questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is reduction potential of hydrogen gas electrode when pure hydrogen gas is at I atmospheric pressure and platinum electrode is in contact with HCl solution of pH 1 at 298 K ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Write the half-cell reaction</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

The reaction at the hydrogen gas electrode is:

$$ \mathrm{H}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{H}_2 $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Here, $n = 1$ (one electron is involved), the standard electrode potential $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}_2}^{\circ} = 0$, and the pressure of hydrogen gas $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 1~\mathrm{atm}$.

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Use the Nernst Equation</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

The reduction potential of the hydrogen electrode is given by:

$$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}_2} = \frac{ -2.303 RT }{ nF } \log_{10} \frac{ \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2}^{1/2} }{ [\mathrm{H}^{+}] } $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Relate pH to $[\mathrm{H}^+]$</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

pH is related to the concentration of hydrogen ions by:

$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10} [\mathrm{H}^{+}]$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Or, $\log_{10} \frac{1}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]} = \mathrm{pH}$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Substitute values</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

Substitute the values into the equation:

$$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}_2} = \frac{-2.303 RT}{nF} \times \mathrm{pH}$$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

At $298~\mathrm{K}$, the value of $\frac{-2.303 RT}{nF}$ is approximately $-0.0592~\mathrm{V}$.

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Given pH = 1:

$$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{H}_2} = -0.0592 \times 1 $$

$$ = -0.0592~\mathrm{V} $$

</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What happens to the emf for the cell, $\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}\left|\mathrm{Zn}_{(1 \mathrm{M})}^{+2} \| \mathrm{Ag}^{+1}(1 \mathrm{M})\right| \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})}^{+}$if concentration of $\mathrm{Ag}^{+1}$ decreases to 0.1 M ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\text { Cell reaction: }\\ &\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}+2 \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}+\mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})} \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{n}=2 \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & E_{\text {cell }}=E_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592}{2} \log \frac{\left[\mathrm{Zn}^{+2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\right]^2} \\ & \left(E_{\text {cell }}\right)_1=E_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592}{2} \log _{10} \frac{[1]}{[1]^2} \\ & \left(E_{\text {cell }}\right)_1=E_{\text {cell }}^{\circ} \quad(\because \log 1=0) \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When concentration of $\mathrm{Ag}^{+}$decreases to 0.1 M .</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }} & =\mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592}{\mathrm{n}} \log \frac{(1)}{(0.1)^2} \\ \mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }} & =\mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592}{2} \times \log \left(10^2\right) \\ & =\mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592}{2} \times 2 \\ & =\left(\mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }}\right)_1-0.0592 \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Above equation indicates the decrease in emf of cell by 0.0592 V when the concentration of $\mathrm{Ag}^{+}$ decreased from 1 M to 0.1 M .</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>For the cell involving following reaction.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{Ni}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}+\mathrm{Ni}_{(\mathrm{s})}, \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{cell}}^*=0.5 \mathrm{~V} . $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>What is standard Gibb's energy change of cell reaction?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The cell reaction:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Zn}_{(s)} + \text{Ni}^{2+}_{(aq)} \;\to\; \text{Zn}^{2+}_{(aq)} + \text{Ni}_{(s)}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.50~\text{V}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>We want the standard Gibbs free energy change, $ \Delta G^\circ $.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Recall the relation</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -n F E^\circ_{\text{cell}}. $</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$n$ = number of moles of electrons transferred.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$F$ = Faraday constant $= 96,500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.50\ \text{V}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Identify electrons exchanged</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Reaction:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Zn(s) → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni(s)</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So, $n = 2$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute values</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -n F E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -(2)(96,500\ \text{C/mol})(0.50\ \text{V}). $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Compute</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -(2)(96,500)(0.50). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = -96,500\ \text{J mol}^{-1}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = -96.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{-96.5\ \text{kJ}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: C</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>If $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)=-0.76 \mathrm{~V}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate potential for $\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{+2}(0.01 \mathrm{M})+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$at 298 K .</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content: <prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}^{0}\left(\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})} \mid \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{eq})}^{+2}\right)=+0.76 \mathrm{~V} \\ & \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}_{\text {electrode }} & =\mathrm{E}_{\text {electrode }}^0-\frac{0.0592}{\mathrm{n}} \log \left[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\right] \\ = & +0.76-\frac{0.0592}{2} \log (0.01) \\ = & +0.76-\frac{0.0592}{2}(-2)=+0.8192 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $\mathrm{E}^o{}\left(\mathrm{AI}_{(\mathrm{eq})}^{+3} \mid \mathrm{AI}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)=-1.66 \mathrm{~V}$. What is potential of $\mathrm{Al}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al}^{+3}(0 \cdot 1 \mathrm{M})+3 \mathrm{e}^{-}$at 298 K ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The given value, $E^o \left(\mathrm{Al}_{(s)} \mid \mathrm{Al}^{3+}_{(aq)}\right) = -1.66~\mathrm{V}$, is the standard potential for the reaction when the concentration of $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is $1~\mathrm{M}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>We are asked to find the potential when $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is at $0.1~\mathrm{M}$ at $298~\mathrm{K}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>We use the Nernst equation to find the new potential:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{electrode}} = E_{\text{electrode}}^o - \frac{0.0592}{n} \log_{10} \frac{[\text{product}]}{[\text{reactant}]} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For this reaction: $\mathrm{Al}_{(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al}^{3+}(0.1~\mathrm{M}) + 3e^{-}$, the only ion to consider is $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ because solid Al does not count in the concentration ratio.</prep-p>
<prep-p>This makes the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{electrode}} = E_{\text{electrode}}^o - \frac{0.0592}{3} \log_{10} [\mathrm{Al}^{3+}] $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Putting $[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}] = 0.1$ and $n = 3$ into the equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{electrode}} = 1.66 - \frac{0.0592}{3} \log_{10}(0.1) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Because $\log_{10}(0.1) = -1$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{electrode}} = 1.66 - (0.0197 \times -1) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{electrode}} = 1.66 + 0.0197 = +1.679~\mathrm{V} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $\mathrm{E}^{\cdot}\left(\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)=-2.37 \mathrm{~V}$. What is potential for $\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{+2}(0.01 \mathrm{M})+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$at 298 K ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\mathrm{E}^p\left(\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})} \mid \mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}\right)=+2.37 \mathrm{~V}\\ &\text { ( } \because \text { reduction potential is given in the question) }\\ &\mathrm{E}_{\text {electrode }}=\mathrm{E}_{\text {electrode }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592}{\mathrm{n}} \log \left[\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\right] \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & =+2.37-\frac{0.0592}{2} \log (0.01) \\ & =+2.37-\frac{0.0592}{2} \times \log 10^{-2} \\ & =+2.37-\frac{0.0592}{2} \times(-2) \\ & =+2.37+0.0592 \\ & =+2.4292 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}{ }_{(\mathrm{aq})} \mid \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)=+0.80 \mathrm{~V}$ What is potential developed for $\mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^{+1}(0.01 \mathrm{M})+\mathrm{e}^{-}$at 298 K ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Nernst equation can be used to calculate electrode potential.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & E_{\text {electrode }}=E_{\text {electrode }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592 \mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{n}} \log _{10} \frac{[\text { Product }]}{[\text { Reactant }]} \\ & E_{\text {electrode }}=E_{\text {electrode }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592 \mathrm{~V}}{1} \log _{10}\left[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\right] \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The standard oxidation potential for given electrode will be 0.80 V</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad & \text { Eelectrode }=-0.8 \mathrm{~V}-\frac{0.0592 \mathrm{~V}}{1} \log _{10} 0.01 \\ & =-0.8 \mathrm{~V}+0.0592 \mathrm{~V} \times(2) \quad\left[\because \log _{10}\left(10^{-2}\right)=-2\right] \\ & =-0.8 \mathrm{~V}+0.1184 \\ & =-0.6816 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>For cell reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 2 \mathrm{Al}_{(\mathrm{s})}+3 \mathrm{Cu}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Al}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+3}+3 \mathrm{Cu}_{(\mathrm{s})} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>If $\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}=-1158 \mathrm{~kJ}$, what is $\mathrm{E}_{\text {cell }}^{\circ}$?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Reaction:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2 \mathrm{Al}_{(s)} + 3 \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}_{(aq)} \;\;\longrightarrow\;\; 2 \mathrm{Al}^{3+}_{(aq)} + 3 \mathrm{Cu}_{(s)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Delta G^\circ = -1158\ \mathrm{kJ} = -1,158,000\ \mathrm{J}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>We need standard cell potential $E^\circ_\text{cell}$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Relation between $\Delta G^\circ$ and $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -n F E^\circ_{\text{cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$n$ = total moles of electrons transferred</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$F \approx 96485\ \mathrm{C/mol}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Electrons transferred in this reaction</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Al goes from 0 to +3: each Al loses 3 e⁻, and there are 2 Al → total 6 electrons.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cu goes from +2 to 0: each Cu²⁺ gains 2 e⁻, and there are 3 Cu²⁺ → total 6 electrons.  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So $n = 6$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Solve for $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{nF} = -\frac{-1{,}158{,}000}{6 \times 96485} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{1{,}158{,}000}{578910} \approx 2.0\ \text{V} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ E^\circ_\text{cell} \approx 2\ \text{V} $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Correct option: B (2 V)</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>What is potential for $\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{+2}(0.1 \mathrm{M})+2 \mathrm{e^-}$ at 298 K ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text {electrode }}=E_{\text {electrode }}^{\circ}-\frac{0.0592 \mathrm{~V}}{n} \log _{10} \frac{[\text { Product }]}{[\text { Reactant }]} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Electrode reaction:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{~s}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(0.1 \mathrm{M})+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Using formula,</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>If standard emf of cell $\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}\left|\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{iM})}^{+2}\right| \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{iM})}^{+1} \mid \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})}$ is 1.55 V .</prep-p>
<prep-p>What is electrical work done under standard conditions?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Standard emf of cell, $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.55\,\text{V}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cell: $\mathrm{Zn_{(s)}|Zn^{2+}_{(1\,M)}||Ag^{+}_{(1\,M)}|Ag_{(s)}}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Write the cell reaction and find $n$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \begin{align*} \text{At anode (oxidation):} &\ \mathrm{Zn(s)} \to \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2e^- \\ \text{At cathode (reduction):} &\ \mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + e^- \to \mathrm{Ag(s)} \\ \end{align*} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>To balance electrons, multiply the cathode reaction by 2:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2\,\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + 2e^- \to 2\,\mathrm{Ag(s)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Overall cell reaction:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\,\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \to \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\,\mathrm{Ag(s)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Formula for maximum electrical work</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Electrical work done under standard conditions is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -nF E^\circ_{\text{cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where,</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$n$ = number of moles of electrons exchanged $(=2)$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$F$ = Faraday’s constant $(=96,500~\text{C/mol})$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ = emf of the cell $(=1.55~\text{V})$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute and calculate</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96,500 \times 1.55 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 149,575 = -299,150~\text{J} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Convert J to kJ:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = \frac{-299,150}{1000}~\text{kJ} = -299.15~\text{kJ} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>The correct answer is:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{-299.150~\text{kJ}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong> is correct.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Assume the cell reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{~A}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}+\mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>if $\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}=-386 \mathrm{~kJ}$ at 298 K . What is $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cell}}^0$ ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cell reaction:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$   \mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}+\mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})}   $$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\Delta G^\circ = -386~\text{kJ} = -386 \times 10^3~\text{J}$ at $T=298~\text{K}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>We are to find $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Write the relationship between $\Delta G^\circ$ and $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -n F E^\circ_{\text{cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$n =$ number of electrons exchanged,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$F =$ Faraday constant $= 96500~\text{C~mol}^{-1}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Find the value of $n$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>From the reaction:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})} \to \mathrm{A}^{2+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + 2e^- $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{B}^{2+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + 2e^- \to \mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $n = 2$ electrons are exchanged.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute the given values in the equation</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ -386 \times 10^3~\text{J} = -2 \times 96500~\text{C~mol}^{-1} \times E^\circ_{\text{cell}} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Solve for $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 386 \times 10^3 = 2 \times 96500 \times E^\circ_{\text{cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{386 \times 10^3}{2 \times 96500} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{386000}{193000} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 2.0~\text{V} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Option C  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{2~\text{V}} $</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Standard potential $\left(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\right)$ of $\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}$ is -0.76 V .</prep-p>
<prep-p>What is standard potential of reaction $2 \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2}+4 \mathrm{e}^{-}$?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-p>Standard reduction potential,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} (aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn} (s),\quad E^\circ = -0.76\,\text{V}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>We need to find the standard potential for:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$2\mathrm{Zn} (s) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} (aq) + 4e^-$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Write the reverse reaction and adjust coefficients</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Original reduction reaction:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} (aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn} (s), \quad E^\circ = -0.76\,\text{V}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Reverse (oxidation) reaction:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mathrm{Zn} (s) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} (aq) + 2e^-$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For the reverse reaction, the standard potential changes sign:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E^\circ_\text{oxidation} = -(-0.76\,\text{V}) = +0.76\,\text{V} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Multiply by 2 (stoichiometric coefficients)</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$2\mathrm{Zn} (s) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} (aq) + 4e^-$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Changing the coefficients does <prep-strong>not</prep-strong> change the value of $E^\circ$ (it depends only on the electrode, not on the number of electrons).</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E^\circ = +0.76\,\text{V} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: $+0.76\,\text{V}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Consider the following cell
$\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$ cell $=1.007 \mathrm{~V}$ and $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$ calomel $=0.242 \mathrm{~V}$ What is the standard potential of Zn ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The standard electrode potential for the cell is given by the equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, the given values are:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$$ \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.007 \, \text{V} $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$$ \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{calomel}} = 0.242 \, \text{V} $$ (this is the calomel electrode, typically used as the reference electrode)</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Assuming the calomel electrode acts as the cathode, we can plug these values into the equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 1.007 \, \text{V} = 0.242 \, \text{V} - \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>To find the standard potential of Zn, rearrange the equation for $$ \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}} $$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}} = 0.242 \, \text{V} - 1.007 \, \text{V} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{E}^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}} = -0.765 \, \text{V} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the standard potential of Zn is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>: $$ -0.765 \, \text{V} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle is executing S.H.M. of amplitude ' $A$ '. When the potential energy of the particle is half of its maximum value during the oscillation, its displacement from the equilibrium position is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The potential energy in simple harmonic motion is given by $P = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The maximum potential energy happens when the particle is at the farthest point from the center. This value is $P_{\max} = \frac{1}{2} k A^2$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>We are told that the current potential energy is half of this maximum value. So,

$$\frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} k A^2 \right)$$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>If we simplify both sides, we get:

$$x^2 = \frac{A^2}{2}$$

So the displacement from the center is:

$$x = \pm \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$$

</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle is executing linear S.H.M. starting from mean position. The ratio of the kinetic energy to the potential energy of the particle at a point of half the amplitude is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>K.E. at half the amplitude position $\left(x=\frac{A}{2}\right)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-\frac{A^2}{4}\right)=\frac{3}{8} m \omega^2 A^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>P.E. at $x=\frac{A}{2}=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{8} m \omega^2 A^2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ The required ratio</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{\text { K.E. }}{\text { P.E. }}=\frac{\left(\frac{3}{8} m \omega^2 A^2\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{8} m \omega^2 A^2\right)}=\frac{3}{1} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle executes S.H.M. starting from the mean position. Its amplitude is ' a ' and its periodic time is ' $T$ '. At a certain instant, its speed ' $u$ ' is half that of maximum speed $\mathrm{V}_{\text {max }}$. The displacement of the particle at that instant is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Speed at displacement x</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ u=\omega \sqrt{a^2-x^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Speed of particle at a certain instant is half that of maximum speed $\mathrm{V}_{\text {max }}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \mathrm{u}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\max }}{2}=\frac{\omega \mathrm{a}}{2} \\ \therefore & \frac{\omega \mathrm{a}}{2}=\omega \sqrt{\mathrm{a}^2-\mathrm{x}^2} \\ & \mathrm{a}^2-\mathrm{x}^2=\frac{\mathrm{a}^2}{4} \\ & \mathrm{x}^2=\frac{3}{4} \mathrm{a}^2 \\ & \mathrm{x}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{a} \end{array} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>For a particle performing S.H.M.; the total energy is ' $n$ ' times the kinetic energy, when the displacement of a particle from mean position is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{~A}$, where A is the amplitude of S.H.M. The value of ' $n$ ' is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We know</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text { K.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \text { and T.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given: T.E. $=\mathrm{n} \times$ K.E.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2=n \times \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \\ & \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2=n \times \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2\left(1-\frac{3}{4}\right) \ldots (given \,\,\,x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} A)\end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & 1=\mathrm{n}\left(1-\frac{3}{4}\right) \\ \therefore & \mathrm{n}=4 \end{array} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>For a particle executing S.H.M. having amplitude A, the speed of the article is $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\text {rd }}$ of its maximum speed when the displacement from the mean position is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& V=\omega \sqrt{A^2-x^2} \quad\text{.... (i)}\\
& V_{\max }=\omega A \\
& V=\frac{V_{\max }}{3}=\frac{\omega a}{3} \\
& \frac{\omega A}{3}=\omega \sqrt{A^2-x^2} \quad\text{... [From (i)]}\\
& \frac{A^2}{9}=\left(A^2-x^2\right) \\
& x^2=A^2-\frac{A^2}{9} \\
& x=\sqrt{\frac{8}{9} A^2} \\
& x=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} A
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle is performing S.H.M. about its mean position with an amplitude ' $a$ ' and periodic time ' $T$ '. The speed of the particle when its displacement from mean position is $\frac{a}{3}$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>In simple harmonic motion (S.H.M.), the displacement of a particle from the mean position is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ x = a \cos(\omega t) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ a $ is the amplitude,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ \omega $ is the angular frequency,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ t $ is the time.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>The angular frequency $\omega$ is related to the periodic time $T$ by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The speed $v$ of a particle performing S.H.M. is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v = \omega \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the displacement $x = \frac{a}{3}$ into the equation, we get:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v = \omega \sqrt{a^2 - \left(\frac{a}{3}\right)^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate $a^2 - \left(\frac{a}{3}\right)^2$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ a^2 - \left(\frac{a}{3}\right)^2 = a^2 - \frac{a^2}{9} = \frac{9a^2}{9} - \frac{a^2}{9} = \frac{8a^2}{9} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the speed $v$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v = \omega \sqrt{\frac{8a^2}{9}} = \omega \cdot a \cdot \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v = \frac{2\pi}{T} \cdot a \cdot \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplifying this expression gives:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v = \frac{4 \sqrt{2} \pi a}{3 T} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the correct answer is Option B:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{4 \sqrt{2} \pi a}{3 T} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle is performing S.H.M. with an amplitude 4 cm . At the mean position the velocity of the particle is $12 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$. When the speed of the particle becomes $6 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$, the distance of the particle from mean position is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{ll} 
& \text { At mean position, } \mathrm{v}_{\max }=\mathrm{A} \omega \\
\therefore & \omega=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\max }}{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{12}{4}=3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\
& \text { Now, } \mathrm{v}=\omega \sqrt{\mathrm{A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2} \\
\therefore & \mathrm{v}^2=\omega^2\left(\mathrm{~A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right) \\
\therefore & \mathrm{x}^2=\mathrm{A}^2-\frac{\mathrm{v}^2}{\omega^2} \\
\therefore \quad & \mathrm{x}=\sqrt{16-\frac{36}{9}}=\sqrt{12}=2 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}
\end{array}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A particle starts from mean position and performs S.H.M. with period 4 second. At what time its kinetic energy is $$50 \%$$ of total energy?</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\left(\cos 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The total energy is given by $$T \cdot E=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{kA}^2$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Kinetic energy is given by $$\mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{k}\left(\mathrm{A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{ll} 
& \text { K.E }=\frac{1}{2} P . E \quad \text{...(given)}\\
\therefore \quad & \frac{1}{2} k\left(A^2-x^2\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\right) \\
\therefore \quad & \left(A^2-x^2\right)=\frac{1}{2} A^2 \\
\therefore \quad & \left(A^2-x^2\right)=\frac{1}{2} A^2 \\
\therefore \quad & x=\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{array}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The equation of displacement in SHM is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{A} \sin \frac{2 \pi \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{T}} \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{A}}{\sqrt{2}}=\mathrm{A} \sin \frac{2 \pi \mathrm{t}}{4} \quad ....(\because \text{T}=\text{4 sec})\\
& \therefore \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sin \frac{\pi \mathrm{t}}{2} \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{\pi \mathrm{t}}{2}=\sin ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
& \quad \frac{\pi \mathrm{t}}{2}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{t}=0.5 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>For a particle executing S.H.M., its potential energy is 8 times its kinetic energy at certain displacement '$$x$$' from the mean position. If '$$A$$' is the amplitude of S.H.M the value of '$$x$$' is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Potential energy: $$U=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2$$ and</prep-p>
<prep-p>Kinetic energy: $$K=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given: Potential energy $$=8 \times$$ Kinetic energy</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{U}=8 \mathrm{~K} \\
& \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2=8 \times \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \\
& x^2=8 A^2-8 x^2 \\
& 9 x^2=8 A^2 \\
& x^2=\frac{8 A^2}{9} \\
& x=\frac{2 \sqrt{2} A}{3} \\
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
questions.sub_topics: The Energy of a Particle Performing S.H.M.

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A body is executing a linear S.H.M. Its potential energies at the displacement '$$\mathrm{x}$$' and '$$\mathrm{y}$$' are '$$\mathrm{E}_1$$' and '$$E_2$$' respectively. Its potential energy at displacement $$(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y})$$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We know,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Potential Energy $$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{Kx}^2$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad \mathrm{E}_1=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{Kx}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{E}_1}{\mathrm{~K}}}$$ .... (i)</prep-p>
<prep-p>and</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$E_2=\frac{1}{2} K y^2 \Rightarrow y=\sqrt{\frac{2 E_2}{K}}$$ ..... (ii)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given, total displacement $$=(x+y)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad$$ Potential energy at displacement $$(x+y)$$,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{E}$$ is $$\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~K}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y})^2$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1}{2} K\left(\sqrt{\frac{2 E_1}{K}}+\sqrt{\frac{2 E_2}{K}}\right)^2 \\
& =\frac{1}{2} K\left[\frac{2 E_1}{K}+\frac{2 E_2}{K}+2\left(\sqrt{\frac{E_1}{K}}\right)\left(\sqrt{\frac{2 E_2}{K}}\right)\right] \\
& =\left(\sqrt{E_1}+\sqrt{E_2}\right)^2=\left(E_1+E_2+2 \sqrt{E_1 E_2}\right)
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The amplitude of a particle executing S.H.M. is $$3 \mathrm{~cm}$$. The displacement at which its kinetic energy will be $$25 \%$$ more than the potential energy is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Given }: \mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E}=\mathrm{P} \cdot \mathrm{E}+\frac{25}{100} \cdot \mathrm{P} \cdot \mathrm{E} \\
& \mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E}=\mathrm{P} \cdot \mathrm{E}+\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{P} \cdot \mathrm{E} \\
& \text { We know K.E }=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2\left(\mathrm{~A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right) \text { and P.E }=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2 \mathrm{x}^2 \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E}=\frac{5}{4} \mathrm{P} \cdot \mathrm{E} \\
& \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2\left(\mathrm{~A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right)=\frac{5}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2 \mathrm{x}^2\right) \\
& \mathrm{A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2=\frac{5}{4} \mathrm{x}^2 \\
& \mathrm{~A}^2=\frac{9}{4} \mathrm{x}^2 \\
\therefore \quad & \mathrm{~A}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{x} \\
\therefore \quad & \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{A} \times \frac{2}{3}=2 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
questions.sub_topics: Amplitude (A), Period (T) and Frequency (N) of S.H.M.

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle is vibrating in S.H.M. with an amplitude of $$4 \mathrm{~cm}$$. At what displacement from the equilibrium position is its energy half potential and half kinetic?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { K.E } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \text { and } \\
\text { P.E } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 \\
\therefore \quad \text { T.E } & =\text { K.E }+ \text { P.E } \\
& =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right)+\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 \\
& =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \\
& \text { Given: K.E }=\text { P.E } \\
\therefore \quad A^2 & -x^2=x^2 \\
\therefore \quad & A^2=2 x^2 \\
\therefore \quad x & =\sqrt{\frac{A^2}{2}}=\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\therefore \quad x & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=2 \sqrt{2} ~\mathrm{c m}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A body is performing S.H.M. of amplitude 'A'. The displacement of the body from a point where kinetic energy is maximum to a point where potential energy is maximum, is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The correct answer is <prep-strong>Option B:  $$ \pm A $$</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Here's why:</prep-p>

<prep-p>In Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM), the total mechanical energy (the sum of kinetic and potential energy) remains constant.  This means that when kinetic energy is at its maximum, potential energy is at its minimum, and vice-versa.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Let's break down the key points:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-strong>Kinetic Energy Maximum:</prep-strong> This occurs when the body is passing through its equilibrium position.  At this point, the velocity is maximum, and therefore kinetic energy is maximum.</prep-li><prep-br>
<prep-li><prep-strong>Potential Energy Maximum:</prep-strong> This occurs at the extreme ends of the motion, where the body momentarily comes to rest.  At these points, the displacement from equilibrium is maximum, and hence potential energy is maximum.</prep-li><prep-br>
<prep-li><prep-strong>Displacement:</prep-strong> The displacement from the point of maximum kinetic energy (equilibrium) to the point of maximum potential energy (extreme position) is exactly equal to the amplitude 'A'.</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Therefore, the displacement is <prep-strong>$$ \pm A $$</prep-strong> (positive or negative depending on the direction of the motion). </prep-p>

<prep-p></prep-p>
questions.sub_topics: The Energy of a Particle Performing S.H.M.

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle excuting S.H.M starts from the mean position. Its amplitude is 'A' and time period '$$\mathrm{T}$$' At what displacement its speed is one-fourth of the maximum speed?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the displacement at which the speed of the particle is one-fourth of its maximum speed, we need to understand the relationship between displacement, amplitude, and velocity in Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM).</prep-p>

<prep-p>In SHM, the velocity $v$ of a particle at a displacement $x$ from the mean position is given by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>$ \omega $ is the angular frequency, and</prep-li>

<prep-li>$ A $ is the amplitude.</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>The angular frequency $ \omega $ is related to the time period $ T $ by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The maximum speed $ v_{max} $ occurs when the particle is at the mean position (i.e., $ x = 0 $), and it is given by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ v_{max} = \omega A $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>We are given that the speed is one-fourth of the maximum speed. Therefore, we can write:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \frac{v_{max}}{4} = \frac{\omega A}{4} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>We need to find the displacement $ x $ at which this condition holds:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \frac{\omega A}{4} = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>We can divide both sides by $ \omega $:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \frac{A}{4} = \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Next, we square both sides to eliminate the square root:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \left(\frac{A}{4}\right)^2 = A^2 - x^2 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>This simplifies to:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \frac{A^2}{16} = A^2 - x^2 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Next, we rearrange the equation to solve for $ x $:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ x^2 = A^2 - \frac{A^2}{16} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ x^2 = \frac{16A^2 - A^2}{16} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ x^2 = \frac{15A^2}{16} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ x = \frac{A \sqrt{15}}{4} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the displacement at which the speed is one-fourth of the maximum speed is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-b>Option D: </prep-b> $$ \frac{\mathrm{A} \sqrt{15}}{40} $$</prep-p>
questions.sub_topics: Acceleration (a), Velocity (v) and Displacement (x) of S.H.M.

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the conductivity of 0.05 M NaOH solution having resistance 31.5 ohm and cell constant $0.315 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$ ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The conductivity ($\kappa$) of a solution can be calculated using the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \kappa = \frac{\text{Cell Constant}}{\text{Resistance}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>Resistance $ R = 31.5 \, \Omega $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Cell Constant $ = 0.315 \, \text{cm}^{-1} $</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Substituting the given values into the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \kappa = \frac{0.315 \, \text{cm}^{-1}}{31.5 \, \Omega} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplifying the above expression:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \kappa = \frac{0.315}{31.5} \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \kappa = 0.01 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the conductivity of the 0.05 M NaOH solution is $0.01 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1}$, which corresponds to Option D.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The conductivity of 0.02 M KCl solution is 0.00250 ohm $^{-1} \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$. What is its molar conductivity?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) is calculated using the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $\kappa$ is the conductivity of the solution, and $c$ is the concentration of the solution in moles per liter (M).</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>Conductivity, $\kappa = 0.00250 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1}$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Concentration, $c = 0.02 \, \text{M}$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Substitute these values into the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Lambda_m = \frac{0.00250 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{-1}}{0.02 \, \text{M}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Perform the division:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Lambda_m = \frac{0.00250}{0.02} \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{2} \, \text{mol}^{-1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Lambda_m = 0.125 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{2} \, \text{mol}^{-1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the molar conductivity is <prep-strong>$125 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{2} \, \text{mol}^{-1}$</prep-strong>. </prep-p>
<prep-p>The correct answer is Option A: </prep-p>
<prep-p>$$125 \, \text{ohm}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^{2} \, \text{mol}^{-1}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The resistance of a conductivity cell of 0.1 M KCl solution is 120 ohm and conductivity is $1.64 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$. What is the value of cell constant?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The cell constant ($G^*$) of a conductivity cell is determined by the relationship between the conductivity ($\kappa$) of the solution and the resistance ($R$) of the cell. The formula for the cell constant is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ G^* = \kappa \times R $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given that the conductivity of the 0.1 M KCl solution is $\kappa = 1.64 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{S \, cm^{-1}}$ and the resistance $R = 120 \, \mathrm{\Omega}$, we can calculate the cell constant as follows:</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the known values into the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ G^* = (1.64 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{S \, cm^{-1}}) \times (120 \, \mathrm{\Omega}) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate the result:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ G^* = 1.64 \times 120 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{cm^{-1}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ G^* = 196.8 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{cm^{-1}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Convert to standard form:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ G^* = 0.01968 \, \mathrm{cm^{-1}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the value of the cell constant is approximately $0.0196 \, \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Hence, the correct option is <prep-strong>Option B: $0.0196 \, \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The electrical conductance of unit volume (1 cm$$^3$$) of solution is called as</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The correct answer is Option D: conductivity.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The electrical conductance of a unit volume (1 cm<prep-sup>3</prep-sup>) of solution is referred to as conductivity. Conductivity is a measure of how well a material can conduct an electric current. It is the inverse of resistivity and is commonly used to describe the ability of solutions to conduct electricity.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the electrical conductance of unit volume (1 cm$$^3$$) of solution is called conductivity.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the conductivity of $$0.02 \mathrm{~M} \mathrm{~KCl}$$ solution if cell constant is $$1.29 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$$ with resistance 645 $$\Omega$$ ?</prep-p>

& \mathrm{R}_{\text {solution }}=645 \Omega, \mathrm{k}=? \\

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Electrical conductance due to all the ions in $$1 \mathrm{~cm}^3$$ of given solution is called as</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The correct answer is Option C: Conductivity.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Electrical conductivity is a measure of the ability of a solution to conduct electric current. It is determined by the presence of ions in the solution, as these ions act as charge carriers. The definition you've provided, which refers to the conductance due to all the ions in $$1 \mathrm{~cm}^3$$ of a given solution, precisely matches the definition of conductivity. Conductivity is usually denoted by the symbol $$\sigma$$ and is the reciprocal of resistivity ($$\rho$$).</prep-p>

<prep-p>To clarify further:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-strong>Molar conductivity</prep-strong> (Option A) refers to the conductivity of a solution containing one mole of electrolyte dissolved in a specified volume of solvent, usually expressed in units of S·cm²/mol. It emphasizes the conductive contribution of the electrolyte on a per-mole basis.</prep-li>

<prep-br/><prep-li><prep-strong>Resistivity</prep-strong> (Option B) is the reciprocal of conductivity. It measures the resistance of a solution to the flow of an electric current, typically denoted by $$\rho$$ and measured in ohm-meters (Ω·m).</prep-li>

<prep-br/><prep-li><prep-strong>Conductivity</prep-strong> (Option C) is the correct answer as per the definition provided in the question. It's a bulk property of the solution and measures how easily electric current can flow through it, generally given in Siemens per meter (S/m).</prep-li>

<prep-br/><prep-li><prep-strong>Electrical conductance</prep-strong> (Option D) is closely related to conductivity but is not the exact answer to the definition provided. Conductance measures the ease with which an electric current passes through an object (not specifically in $$1 \mathrm{~cm}^3$$), denoted by G and measured in Siemens (S).</prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p>Therefore, conductivity most accurately fits the description of the electrical conductance due to all ions in $$1 \mathrm{~cm}^3$$ of a given solution.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Molar conductivity of 0.04 M BaCl$$_2$$ solution is 230 $$\Omega^{-1}$$ cm$$^2$$ mol$$^{-1}$$ at 27$$^\circ$$C. What is it's conductivity?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the conductivity (κ) of the 0.04 M BaCl$$_2$$ solution, we use the relationship between molar conductivity ($$\Lambda_m$$) and conductivity (κ). The formula is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Where:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>$$\Lambda_m$$ is the molar conductivity</prep-li>

<prep-li>κ is the conductivity</prep-li>

<prep-li>c is the concentration of the solution in mol/L</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>$$\Lambda_m = 230~\Omega^{-1}~\text{cm}^2~\text{mol}^{-1}$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>c = 0.04 M</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>We need to find κ. Rearrange the formula to solve for κ:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\kappa = \Lambda_m \times c$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Substitute the given values:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\kappa = 230~\Omega^{-1}~\text{cm}^2~\text{mol}^{-1} \times 0.04~\text{mol}~\text{L}^{-1}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\kappa = 9.2~\Omega^{-1}~\text{cm}^{-1}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>So the correct answer is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option B</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{9.2\times10^{-3}~\Omega^{-1}~cm^{-1}}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A complex reaction takes place in following steps.</prep-p>

<prep-p>For a complex reaction, rate law can be written as law of mass action for the rate determining step.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the average rate of reaction when change in concentration of product is 0.05 M in 20 seconds?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The average rate of reaction tells us how fast the amount of product changes over time.</prep-p>
<prep-p>To find the average rate, use this formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\text{Average rate} = \frac{\Delta[\text{Product}]}{\Delta t}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, $\Delta[\text{Product}]$ is the change in concentration of the product, which is $0.05\,\mathrm{M}$, and $\Delta t$ is the time taken, which is $20\,\mathrm{s}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, substitute the values into the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\text{Average rate} = \frac{0.05\,\mathrm{M}}{20\,\mathrm{s}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Do the division:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\text{Average rate} = 0.0025\,\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, the average rate of reaction is $0.0025\,\mathrm{M}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A reaction is first order with respective to $$\mathrm{A}$$ and second order with respective to $$\mathrm{B}$$. What is the effect on reaction rate if concentration of B is increased 3 times?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the effect on the reaction rate when the concentration of $$\mathrm{B}$$ is increased 3 times, we need to consider the rate law for the reaction. A reaction that is first order with respect to $$\mathrm{A}$$ and second order with respect to $$\mathrm{B}$$ has a rate law given by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^1[\mathrm{B}]^2$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Here, $ k $ is the rate constant, $[\mathrm{A}]$ is the concentration of reactant $$\mathrm{A}$$, and $[\mathrm{B}]$ is the concentration of reactant $$\mathrm{B}$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>According to the problem, the concentration of $$\mathrm{B}$$ is increased 3 times. Let’s denote the initial concentration of $$\mathrm{B}$$ as $[\mathrm{B}]_0$. After increasing the concentration, the new concentration of $$\mathrm{B}$$ becomes:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ [\mathrm{B}]_{\text{new}} = 3[\mathrm{B}]_0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now we substitute this new concentration into the rate law:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \text{Rate}_{\text{new}} = k[\mathrm{A}]_0(3[\mathrm{B}]_0)^2 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Simplifying the expression, we get:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \text{Rate}_{\text{new}} = k[\mathrm{A}]_0 \cdot 9[\mathrm{B}]_0^2 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \text{Rate}_{\text{new}} = 9 \cdot k[\mathrm{A}]_0[\mathrm{B}]_0^2 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>This shows that the new rate is 9 times the initial reaction rate. Thus, the reaction rate increases by a factor of 9 when the concentration of $$\mathrm{B}$$ is increased 3 times.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the correct answer is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong> Rate increases 9 times</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The rate law equation for a reaction between $$\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$$ and $$\mathrm{C}$$ is $$\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}][\mathrm{C}]^2$$, what will be ne rate of reaction if concentration of both $$\mathrm{A}$$ and $$\mathrm{B}$$ are doubled.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the new rate of the reaction when the concentrations of both $$\mathrm{A}$$ and $$\mathrm{B}$$ are doubled, we start with the given rate law equation:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{r} = \mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}][\mathrm{C}]^2$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now, let's say initially, the concentrations of $$\mathrm{A}$$, $$\mathrm{B}$$, and $$\mathrm{C}$$ are $$[\mathrm{A}]$$, $$[\mathrm{B}]$$, and $$[\mathrm{C}]$$ respectively. If the concentrations of $$\mathrm{A}$$ and $$\mathrm{B}$$ are doubled, the new concentrations will be:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$2[\mathrm{A}]$$ and $$2[\mathrm{B}]$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>We substitute these new concentrations back into the rate law equation to find the new rate $$\mathrm{r_{new}}$$:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{r_{new}} = \mathrm{k}[(2[\mathrm{A}])][(2[\mathrm{B}])][\mathrm{C}]^2$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now we simplify this expression:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{r_{new}} = \mathrm{k} \cdot 2[\mathrm{A}] \cdot 2[\mathrm{B}] \cdot [\mathrm{C}]^2$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{r_{new}} = 4\left(\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}][\mathrm{C}]^2\right)$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Since $$\mathrm{r} = \mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}][\mathrm{C}]^2$$, we can substitute $$\mathrm{r}$$ for $$\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}][\mathrm{C}]^2$$:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{r_{new}} = 4\mathrm{r}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the new rate of the reaction is $$4\mathrm{r}$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The correct answer is Option B: $$4 \mathrm{r}$$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the rate of disappearance of B in following reaction? $$2 \mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{C}$$, if rate of appearance of $$\mathrm{C}$$ is $$1.3 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the rate of appearance of $$\mathrm{Z}$$ in following reaction? $$3 \mathrm{x} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{y}+\mathrm{z}$$, if rate of disappearance of $$\mathrm{x}$$ is $$0.072 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Equation of the plane passing through $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ and parallel to $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& \overline{\mathrm{r}} \cdot(\overline{\mathrm{~b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}})  =\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot(\overline{\mathrm{~b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \\
& \therefore \quad\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathrm{i}} & \hat{\mathrm{j}} \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\
3 & 2 & -4 \\
2 & -3 & 2
\end{array}\right|=-8 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-14 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-13 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\
\therefore & \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot(\overline{\mathrm{~b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}) =(2)(-8)+(-1)(-14)+(-3)(-13) \\
& =-16+14+39=37
\end{array}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ Required equation is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { r} \cdot(-8 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-14 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-13 \hat{\mathrm{k}})=37 \\
& \text { i.e., } 8 x+14 y+13 z+37=0
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$4 \lambda+1=\mu$$ ..... (3)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting value of $$\mu$$ from (3) in (1), we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& 2 \lambda+1=(4 \lambda+1)+3 \Rightarrow 2 \lambda=-3 \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-3}{2} \\

\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting values of $$\lambda$$ and $$\mu$$ in (2), we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$3\left(\frac{-3}{2}\right)-1=2(-5)+k \quad \Rightarrow k=\frac{9}{2}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>If lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}$ and $\frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-\lambda}{2}=\frac{z}{1}$ intersect each other, then $\lambda=\ldots \ldots$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p> Given lines are</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}=\lambda_1 \text { (let) }\quad\text{.... (i)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>and $\frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-\lambda}{2}=\frac{z}{1}=\lambda_2$ (let) ... (ii)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Then, any point on line (i) is $\left(2 \lambda_1+1,3 \lambda_1-1,4 \lambda_1+1\right)$ and any point on line (ii) is $\left(\lambda_2+3,2 \lambda_2+\lambda, \lambda_2\right)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Clearly, then lines (i) and (ii) will intersect if 
$$\left(2 \lambda_1+1,3 \lambda_1-1,4 \lambda_1+1\right)=\left(\lambda_2+3,2 \lambda_2+\lambda, \lambda_2\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For some particular value of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 \lambda_1+1=\lambda_2+3,3 \lambda_1-1=2 \lambda_2+\lambda \\
& \text { and } 4 \lambda_1+1=\lambda_2 \\
& \Rightarrow 2 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=2,3 \lambda_1-2 \lambda_2=\lambda+1 \text { and } 4 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=-1
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>On solving $2 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=2$ and $4 \lambda_1-\lambda_2=-1$ We get $\lambda_1=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $\lambda_2=-5$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, putting the values of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ in</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& 3 \lambda_1-2 \lambda_2 =\lambda+1 \\
\Rightarrow & 3\left(\frac{-3}{2}\right)-2(-5) =\lambda+1 \Rightarrow \frac{-9}{2}+10=\lambda+1 \\
\Rightarrow & \lambda+1 =\frac{11}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{9}{2}
\end{array}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: Calculate the work done in joule if 1 mole of an ideal gas compressed from volume $24 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $13 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant external pressure 3 bar.
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall formula</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Work of expansion/compression at constant external pressure:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ w = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Volumes</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Initial volume:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_i = 24~\text{dm}^3 $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Final volume:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_f = 13~\text{dm}^3 $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Change in volume:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta V = V_f - V_i = 13 - 24 = -11~\text{dm}^3 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: External pressure (convert units)</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ P_{\text{ext}} = 3~\text{bar} $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Recall:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 1~\text{bar·dm}^3 = 100~\text{J} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Work calculation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ w = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V = - (3~\text{bar})(-11~\text{dm}^3) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ w = 33~\text{bar·dm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Convert to joule:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ w = 33 \times 100 = 3300~\text{J} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The work done is <prep-strong>3300 J</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: A (3300 J)</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the work done in joule if 1 mole of ideal gas is compressed from $25 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $13 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant external pressure 4 bar.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>First, we are given:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$V_1 = 25~\mathrm{dm}^3$ (initial volume), $V_2 = 13~\mathrm{dm}^3$ (final volume), and the external pressure $P_\mathrm{ext} = 4~\mathrm{bar}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Work done by the gas when compressed at constant external pressure can be found using:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$W = -P_\mathrm{ext} \Delta V = -P_\mathrm{ext} (V_2 - V_1)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, substitute the values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$W = -4~\mathrm{bar} \times (13~\mathrm{dm}^3 - 25~\mathrm{dm}^3)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$13 - 25 = -12$, so $W = -4~\mathrm{bar} \times (-12~\mathrm{dm}^3)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculating this, $W = 48~\mathrm{dm}^3\,\mathrm{bar}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Next, we need to convert $48~\mathrm{dm}^3\,\mathrm{bar}$ to joules. We know that $1~\mathrm{dm}^3\,\mathrm{bar} = 100~\mathrm{J}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $W = 48~\mathrm{dm}^3\,\mathrm{bar} \times 100~\mathrm{J}/(\mathrm{dm}^3\,\mathrm{bar}) = 4800~\mathrm{J}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the work done in joule if 2 moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally from $15.5 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $20 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at constant pressure 1 atm .</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall the work expression</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For expansion work against external constant pressure:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ w = -P_{\text{ext}} \, \Delta V $</prep-p>
<prep-p>(Sign convention: in chemistry, work done <prep-em>by</prep-em> the system is taken as negative.)</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Extract quantities</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Initial volume:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_1 = 15.5 \,\text{dm}^3 = 15.5 \times 10^{-3} \,\text{m}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Final volume:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_2 = 20 \,\text{dm}^3 = 20 \times 10^{-3} \,\text{m}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Change in volume:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta V = (20-15.5)\,\text{dm}^3 = 4.5 \,\text{dm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Convert to liters/m³:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $1 \,\text{dm}^3 = 1 \, L$: $\Delta V = 4.5 \, L$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Also, $1 \, L = 10^{-3} \, \text{m}^3$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $\Delta V = 4.5 \times 10^{-3} \,\text{m}^3$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Pressure in SI units</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ 1 \,\text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5 \, \text{Pa} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Work Calculation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ w = -P \Delta V = -(1.013 \times 10^5)(4.5 \times 10^{-3}) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ w = -(1.013 \times 10^5 \times 0.0045) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = -(456) \,\text{J} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 5: Match with options</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The closest option is: <prep-strong>A: -456 J</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Final Answer: Option A (-456 J)</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the constant external pressure required to expand 2 moles of an ideal gas from volume $15 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $20 \mathrm{dm}^3$ if amount of work done is -600 J .</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Initial volume, $V_1 = 15 \ \mathrm{dm}^3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Final volume, $V_2 = 20 \ \mathrm{dm}^3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Amount of work done, $w = -600 \ \mathrm{J}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Number of moles, $n = 2$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Write the formula for work done at constant pressure, $P_{ext}$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>For expansion at constant external pressure:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ w = -P_{ext} \Delta V $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Calculate $\Delta V$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 20 \ \mathrm{dm}^3 - 15 \ \mathrm{dm}^3 = 5 \ \mathrm{dm}^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Convert $\mathrm{dm}^3$ to $\mathrm{m}^3$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 1 \ \mathrm{dm}^3 = 1 \times 10^{-3} \ \mathrm{m}^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta V = 5 \ \mathrm{dm}^3 = 5 \times 10^{-3} \ \mathrm{m}^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute values into the work formula and solve for $P_{ext}$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ w = -P_{ext} \Delta V $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given $w = -600 \ \mathrm{J}$, so:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ -600 = -P_{ext} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide both sides by $-1$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 600 = P_{ext} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{ext} = \frac{600}{5 \times 10^{-3}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{ext} = \frac{600}{0.005} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{ext} = 120000 \ \mathrm{Pa} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Convert $\mathrm{Pa}$ to $\mathrm{bar}$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 1 \ \mathrm{bar} = 10^5 \ \mathrm{Pa} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{ext} = \frac{120000}{100000} = 1.2 \ \mathrm{bar} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A:</prep-strong> $1.2 \ \mathrm{bar}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Find the constant external pressure required to expand a gas from 2.5 L to 4.5 L if amount of work done is 500 J at 298 K ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{V}_1 & =2.5 \mathrm{~L}, \mathrm{~V}_2=4.5 \mathrm{~L}, \\
\mathrm{~W} & =-500 \mathrm{~J}=-5 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\left(\because 100 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\right) \\
\mathrm{W} & =-\mathrm{P}_{\text {ext }} \Delta \mathrm{V} \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ext}} & =-\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\Delta \mathrm{~V}}=-\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\left(\mathrm{~V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right)} \\
& =\frac{-\left(-5 \mathrm{dm}^3 \text { bar }\right)}{(4.5-2.5) \mathrm{dm}^3}=2.5 \mathrm{bar}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>2 moles of an ideal gas expands isothermally from $5 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $10 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at a constant external pressure of 1.5 bar. Calculate work done.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To calculate the work done by an ideal gas during isothermal expansion at constant external pressure, the formula used is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ W $ is the work done by the gas,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ P_{\text{ext}} $ is the constant external pressure,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ \Delta V $ is the change in volume.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ P_{\text{ext}} = 1.5 \, \text{bar} $,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Initial volume, $ V_i = 5 \, \text{dm}^3 $,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Final volume, $ V_f = 10 \, \text{dm}^3 $.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>First, calculate the change in volume:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta V = V_f - V_i = 10 \, \text{dm}^3 - 5 \, \text{dm}^3 = 5 \, \text{dm}^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, plug in the values into the work formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -1.5 \, \text{bar} \times 5 \, \text{dm}^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -7.5 \, \text{dm}^3 \, \text{bar} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the work done by the gas is $-7.5 \, \text{dm}^3 \, \text{bar}$. </prep-p>
<prep-p>The correct answer is Option B: </prep-p>
<prep-p>$-7.5 \, \text{dm}^3 \, \text{bar}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two moles of an ideal gas is expanded isothermally from a volume of $300 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ to 2.5 $\mathrm{dm}^3$ at 298 K against a constant pressure at 1.9 bar. Calculate the work done in joules.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To calculate the work done when an ideal gas expands isothermally against a constant pressure, the formula to use is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ W $ is the work done by the gas (negative when the gas does work on the surroundings).</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ P_{\text{ext}} $ is the external pressure (in pascals).</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ \Delta V $ is the change in volume (in cubic meters).</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step-by-Step Calculation:</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Convert Volumes to Appropriate Units:</prep-strong></prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-p>Initial volume: $ V_1 = 300 \, \mathrm{cm}^3 = 300 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{m}^3 = 0.0003 \, \mathrm{m}^3 $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Final volume: $ V_2 = 2.5 \, \mathrm{dm}^3 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \, \mathrm{m}^3 = 0.0025 \, \mathrm{m}^3 $</prep-p></prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Calculate the Change in Volume:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta V = V_2 - V_1 = 0.0025 \, \mathrm{m}^3 - 0.0003 \, \mathrm{m}^3 = 0.0022 \, \mathrm{m}^3 $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Convert Pressure to Pascals:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The pressure is given as $ 1.9 \, \text{bar} $. Convert this to pascals knowing that $ 1 \, \text{bar} = 10^5 \, \text{Pa} $.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{\text{ext}} = 1.9 \, \text{bar} = 1.9 \times 10^5 \, \text{Pa} $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Calculate the Work Done:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Using the formula for work:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V = -(1.9 \times 10^5 \, \mathrm{Pa})(0.0022 \, \mathrm{m}^3) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -(1.9 \times 10^5 \times 0.0022) \, \mathrm{J} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -418 \, \mathrm{J} $$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>The work done during the isothermal expansion of the gas is $-418 \, \mathrm{J}$. Therefore, the correct answer is Option A: $-418 \, \mathrm{J}$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A gas absorbs certain amount of heat and expands by $200 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ against a constant external pressure of $2 \times 10^5 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$. What is work done by system?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The work done by a system during an isobaric process (constant pressure) can be calculated using the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -P \Delta V $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$W$ is the work done by the system,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$P$ is the external pressure,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$\Delta V$ is the change in volume.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$P = 2 \times 10^5 \, \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$\Delta V = 200 \, \mathrm{cm}^3$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>First, convert the change in volume from $\mathrm{cm}^3$ to $\mathrm{m}^3$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta V = 200 \, \mathrm{cm}^3 = 200 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{m}^3 = 2 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{m}^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the values into the work formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -(2 \times 10^5 \, \mathrm{Nm}^{-2})(2 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{m}^3) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ W = -4 \times 10^1 \, \mathrm{J} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the work done by the system is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B:</prep-strong> $-40.53 \, \mathrm{J}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A gas is allowed to expand against a constant external pressure of 2.5 bar from an initial volume 'x' L to final volume of 4.5 L. If amount of work done is 5 dm$$^3$$ bar, what is the value of 'x'?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{at}}=2.5 \text { bar, } \mathrm{V}_1=\mathrm{x} \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{V}_2=4.5 \mathrm{~L} \\
& \mathrm{~W}=-5 \mathrm{~dm}^3 \text { bar }=-5 \mathrm{~L} \text { bar } \\
& \qquad \mathrm{W}=-\mathrm{P}_{\text {ext }}\left(\mathrm{V}_2-\mathrm{V}_1\right) \\
& \therefore-5 \mathrm{~L} \text { bar }=-2.5 \text { bar }(4.5-\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{L} \\
& \therefore \quad 5 \mathrm{~L} \text { bar }=11.25 \mathrm{~L} \text { bar }-2.5 \times \mathrm{L} \text { bar } \\
& \therefore 2.5 \times \mathrm{L} \text { bar }=(11.25-5) \mathrm{L} \text { bar } \\
& \therefore \quad \quad \mathrm{x}=\frac{6.25}{2.5} \quad=2.5
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the time required for $99 \%$ completion of a first order reaction if rate constant is $23.03 \mathrm{~min}^{-1}$ ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{t}=\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{k}} \log _{10} \frac{[\mathrm{~A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$99 \%$ of reaction is complete, so if $[\mathrm{A}]_0=100$,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & {[\mathrm{A}]_{\mathrm{t}}=100-99=1 } \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{t} & =\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{k}} \log _{10} \frac{(100)}{(1)} \\ & =\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{k}} \times 2=\frac{2.303}{23.03} \times 2=0.2 \text { minutes } \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate rate constant of first order reaction if concentration of reactant decreases by $90 \%$ in 30 minute?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Concentration decreases by $90 \%$. Hence, $10 \%$ reactant is left after 30 minutes.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{k} & =\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{t}} \log _{10} \frac{[\mathrm{~A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}} \\
\mathrm{k} & =\frac{2.303}{30} \log _{10} \frac{100}{10} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{30 \mathrm{~min}}=7.67 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~min}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>For a reaction $$\mathrm{A} \rightarrow$$ product, rate constant is $$2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$$. The initial concentration of $$\mathrm{A}$$ is 1.0 mol dm$${ }^{-3}$$. What is the value of $$\log \frac{1}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}}$$ after 100 seconds?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{k}=2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}, \quad[\mathrm{~A}]_0=1.0 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{dm}{ }^{-3}, \mathrm{t}=100 \mathrm{~s}, \quad \log \frac{1}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}}=?$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& k=\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{t}} \log _{10} \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}} \\
\therefore \quad & \log _{10} \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}}=\frac{\mathrm{k} \times \mathrm{t}}{2.303} \\
\therefore \quad & \log _{10} \frac{1}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-2} \times 100}{2.303}=0.868 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~dm}^{-3}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the half-life of a first order reaction if time required to decrease concentration of reactant from 1.0 M to 0.25 M is 10 hour?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{t}=10$$ hour, $$[\mathrm{A}]_0=1.0 \mathrm{M},[\mathrm{A}]_{\mathrm{t}}=0.25 \mathrm{M}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>(i) $$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{k} & =\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{t}} \log _{10} \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}} & =\frac{2.303}{10 \mathrm{~h}} \log _{10} \frac{1.0}{0.25} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{10 \mathrm{~h}} \log _{10} 4 & =\frac{2.303 \times 0.6020}{10 \mathrm{~h}} \\
& =0.139 \mathrm{~h}^{-1} &
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>(ii) $$\begin{aligned}
t_{1 / 2} & =\frac{0.693}{k} & =\frac{0.693}{0.139 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}} \\
& =4.98 \text { hour } & \approx 5 \text { hours }
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>For first order reaction the concentration of reactant decreases from 0.2 to 0.1 M in 100 minutes. What is the rate constant of the reaction?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Time}(t) & =100 \mathrm{~min} \\
{\left[A_0\right] } & =0.2 \mathrm{M} \\
{[A] } & =0.1 \mathrm{M}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>According first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { rate constant }(k)=\frac{2.303}{t} \log \frac{\left[A_0\right]}{[A]} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{100 \mathrm{~min}} \log \frac{[0.2]}{[0.1]} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{100 \min } \times 0.3010[\because \log 2=0.3010] \\
& =6.93 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~min}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A first order reaction has a rate constant 0.00813 min$$^{-1}$$. How long will it take for 60% completion?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Rate constant $$(k)=0.00813 \mathrm{~min}^{-1}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>According to first order reaction, the relation is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
t & =\frac{2.303}{k} \log \frac{a}{a-x} \\
\text { As, } \quad a & =100,(a-x)=100-60=40 \\
\therefore \quad t & =\frac{2.303}{0.00813} \log \frac{100}{40} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{0.00813} \times \log 2.5 \quad[\log 2.5=0.3979] \\
& =112.7 \mathrm{~min}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the value of rate constant of first order reaction, if it takes 15 minutes for consumption of $$20 \%$$ of reactants?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given, $$t=15 \mathrm{~min}$$ for $$20 \%$$ of reactant to react.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Rate constant $$(k)=\frac{.2 .303}{t} \log \frac{\left[R_0\right]}{[R]}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where,</prep-p>
<prep-p>[$$R_0]=$$ original amount of reactant</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$[R]=$$ reactant remaining unreacted</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { So, }\left[R_0\right] & =100 \\
{[R] } & =80(20 \% \text { reacted }) \\
k & =\frac{2.303}{15 \mathrm{~min}} \log \left[\frac{100}{80}\right] \\
& =1.48 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~min}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A first order reaction has rate constant $$1 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$$. What time will, it take for $$20 \mathrm{~g}$$ or reactant to reduce to $$5 \mathrm{~g}$$ ?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Rate constant $$(k)=1 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Initial concentration $$(a)=20 \mathrm{~g}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Final concentration $$(a-x)=5 g$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Rate constant $$(k)=\frac{2.303}{t} \log \left(\frac{a}{a-x}\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>In terms of time,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$t=\frac{2.303}{k} \log \left(\frac{a}{a-x}\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Putting the values,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$t=\frac{2.303}{1 \times 10^{-2}} \log \left(\frac{20}{5}\right)=138.6 \mathrm{~s}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Hence, the time required will be $$138.6 \mathrm{~s}$$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The equation of the plane, passing through the point $(1,1,1)$ and perpendicular to the planes $2 x+y-2 z=5$ and $3 x-6 y-2 z=7$, is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The equation of plane passing through $(1,1,1)$ is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$a(x-1)+b(y-1)+c(z-1)=0\quad\text{... (i)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since plane (i) is perpendicular to the planes</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$2 x+y-2 z=5 \text { and } 3 x-6 y-2 z=7$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore \quad & 2 a+b-2 c=5 \quad\text{.... (ii)}\\
& 3 a-6 b-2 c=7 \quad\text{.... (iii)}
\end{array}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>On solving (i), (ii) and (iii), we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$a=14, b=2, c=15$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the values of $a, b, c$ in (i), we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& 14(x-1)+2(y-1)+15(z-1)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 14 x+2 y+15 z=31
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The equation of the plane passing through the point $(1,1,1)$ and perpendicular to the planes $2 x-y-2 z=5$ and $3 x-6 y+2 z=7$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:

<prep-p>Equation of required plane is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \left|\begin{array}{ccc}
x-1 & y-1 & z-1 \\
2 & -1 & -2 \\
3 & -6 & 2
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(x-1)(-14)-(y-1)(10) \\
& \quad+(z-1)(-12+3)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow-14 x+14-10 y+10-9 z+9=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 14 x+10 y+9 z=-33
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Equation of the plane passing through $$(1,-1,2)$$ and perpendicular to the planes $$x+2 y-2 z=4$$ and $$3 x+2 y+z=6$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The equation of plane passing through $$(1,-1,2)$$ is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{a}(x-1)+\mathrm{b}(y+1)+\mathrm{c}(\mathrm{z}-2)=0$$ ..... (i)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since plane (i) is perpendicular to the planes $$x+2 y-2 z=4$$ and $$3 x+2 y+z=6$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad a+2 b-2 c=0 \\
& \text { and } 3 a+2 b+c=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{a}{6}=\frac{b}{-7}=\frac{c}{-4}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad$$ The equation of the required plane is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& 6(x-1)-7(y+1)-4(z-2)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 6 x-7 y-4 z-5=0
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The equation of the line, passing through $$(1,2,3)$$ and parallel to planes $$x-y+2 z=5$$ and $$3 x+y+z=6$$, is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Required equation of line is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{x-1}{\left|\begin{array}{cc}
-1 & 2 \\
1 & 1
\end{array}\right|}=\frac{y-2}{-\left|\begin{array}{cc}
1 & 2 \\

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The Cartesian equation of a line passing through $$(1,2,3)$$ and parallel to $$x-y+2 z=5$$ and $$3 x+y+z=6$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Required line $$L \rightarrow P(1,2,3)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& L \| E_1: 1 x-1 y+2 z=5 \\
& L \| E_2: 3 x+1 y+1 z=6
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\overline{n_1} \equiv(1,-1,2), \overline{n_2} \equiv(3,1,1)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \overline{n_1} \times \overline{n_2} & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\boldsymbol{i}} & \hat{\boldsymbol{j}} & \hat{\boldsymbol{k}} \\
1 & -1 & 2 \\
3 & 1 & 1
\end{array}\right|=-3 \hat{\boldsymbol{i}}-5 \hat{\boldsymbol{j}}+4 \hat{\boldsymbol{k}} \\
& \equiv(-3,-5,4)
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore$$ d.R.s. of line $$L$$ are $$(-3,-5,4)$$ and it passes through $$(1,2,3)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore$$ its cartesian equations are</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{x-1}{-3}=\frac{y-2}{-5}=\frac{z-3}{4}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Normal of plane perpendicular to given plane is,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} & +3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \times(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \\
& =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
2 & 3 & -2 \\
1 & 2 & -3
\end{array}\right|=-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Equation of plane passing through $(1,-1,2)$ and whose normal vector $-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$, is</prep-p>

& (\mathbf{r}-(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \cdot(-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=0 \\
& \mathbf{r} \cdot(5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}})=-(-5-4+2) \\
& \mathbf{r} \cdot(5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}})=7
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
