questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The equation of the plane passing through the points $$(2,3,1),(4,-5,3)$$ and parallel to $$X$$-axis is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To find the equation of a plane passing through two points and parallel to the X-axis, we need to understand that a plane parallel to the X-axis would have a normal vector that is orthogonal (perpendicular) to the X-axis. Since the X-axis is represented by the vector $$(1, 0, 0)$$, any normal vector to the plane will have the form $$(0, b, c)$$, where $$b$$ and $$c$$ are real numbers. This means that the plane's normal vector does not have an X component.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The general equation of a plane in three dimensions is given by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where $$(x_0, y_0, z_0)$$ is a point on the plane, and $$ (A, B, C) $$ is a normal vector to the plane.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Since the plane is parallel to the X-axis, we know that $$ A = 0 $$. Therefore, the equation simplifies to:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now we need to find values for $$ B $$ and $$ C $$ that will allow the plane to pass through $$ (2,3,1) $$ and $$ (4,-5,3) $$. These two points will provide us the direction vectors along the plane:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>
<prep-li>From point $$ (2,3,1) $$ to $$ (4,-5,3) $$, we get the direction vector by subtracting the respective components:</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$$ (4 - 2, -5 - 3, 3 - 1) = (2, -8, 2) $$.</prep-p>

<prep-ul>
<prep-li>However, we need a direction vector that lies on the plane and is perpendicular to the X-axis direction vector. Given that the plane is parallel to the X-axis, the direction vector of the plane can simply be taken from the YZ components of the direction vector we found:</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$$ (0, -8, 2) $$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now we can normalize this vector to get the plane's normal vector. Multiplying by a constant does not change the direction, so we can use $$(0, B, C) = (0, -8, 2)$$ directly or choose to simplify it by dividing by a common factor, for instance, dividing by 2 to get $$(0, -4, 1)$$ so:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (B, C) = (-4, 1) $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now let's use one of the given points, $(2, 3, 1)$, to find the equation:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ -4(y - 3) + 1(z - 1) = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ -4y + 12 + z - 1 = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ -4y + z + 11 = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>This can be rearranged to:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 4y - z = 11 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>So the correct equation of the plane should be:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 4y - z = 11 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>This is not present in the given options. Let's check the options to see if any of them would be equivalent:</prep-p>

<prep-p>If we consider Option A, we get:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 3y + 4z = 13 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>For this equation to represent the same plane as $$ 4y - z = 11 $$, we would need the ratio between coefficients of $$ y $$ and $$ z $$ to be the same, and the independent term to scale accordingly.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Let's evaluate this by putting $$ y $$ and $$ z $$ from the point $$(2, 3, 1)$$ into Option A:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 3(3) + 4(1) = 9 + 4 = 13 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option A satisfies the point $$(2, 3, 1)$$. Now we need to do the same for the second point $$(4, -5, 3)$$:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 3(-5) + 4(3) = -15 + 12 = -3 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>But for this plane,</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 4y - z = 11 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 4(-5) - 3 = -20 - 3 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ -23 \neq 11 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Hence Option A does not represent the same plane as $$ 4y - z = 11 $$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option B:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ y - 4z = -1 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Using the given points we can test for Option B in a similar fashion:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (2, 3, 1): \quad 3 - 4(1) = 3 - 4 = -1 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (4, -5, 3): \quad -5 - 4(3) = -5 - 12 = -17 \neq -1 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>So, Option B can be ruled out as well.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Performing a similar verification for Options C and D:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option C:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 2y + 4z = 19 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Using the given points:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (2, 3, 1): \quad 2(3) + 4(1) = 6 + 4 = 10 \neq 19 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (4, -5, 3): \quad 2(-5) + 4(3) = -10 + 12 = 2 \neq 19 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option C is not the correct option.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option D:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ y + 4z = 7 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Using the given points:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (2, 3, 1): \quad 3 + 4(1) = 3 + 4 = 7 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ (4, -5, 3): \quad -5 + 4(3) = -5 + 12 = 7 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option D works with both points. Moreover, the ratio of coefficients between $$ y $$ and $$ z $$ in our correct equation $$ 4y - z = 11 $$ is 4 to -1. We can invert this to get -1 to 4, which matches the ratio for the coefficients of $$ y $$ and $$ z $$ in Option D, after rearranging it to be $$ y + 4z - 7 = 0 $$. This indicates that Option D could represent the same plane as our equation but with the terms moved around.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Based upon this analysis, the correct answer should be:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option D</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ y + 4z = 7 $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>If the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the origin to a plane is $\mathrm{P}(2,-1,4)$, then the equation of the plane is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall the concept</prep-h3>
<prep-p>If $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from a point $O(0,0,0)$ to a plane, then:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Vector $OP = (2, -1, 4)$ is perpendicular to the plane (i.e. it is parallel to the plane’s normal).</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Therefore, the plane has a normal vector $n = (2, -1, 4)$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>The plane passes through $P(2, -1, 4)$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So the equation of the plane:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n \cdot \big((x,y,z) - P\big) = 0. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Write the equation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ (2, -1, 4) \cdot ( (x-2), (y+1), (z-4) ) = 0 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2(x-2) + (-1)(y+1) + 4(z-4) = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2x - 4 - y - 1 + 4z - 16 = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2x - y + 4z - 21 = 0. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Match the option</prep-h3>
<prep-p>That corresponds to <prep-strong>Option D</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>The equation of the plane is  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{2x - y + 4z - 21 = 0} \quad (\text{Option D}) $</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The foot of the perpendicular drawn from origin to a plane is $\mathrm{M}(2,1,-2)$, then vector equation of the plane is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The equation of a plane passing through a point $\text{M}(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ with normal vector $\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c \rangle$ is given by the vector equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \overline{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{OM} \cdot \mathbf{n} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $\overline{\mathbf{r}}$ is the position vector of any point $(x, y, z)$ on the plane, and $\mathbf{OM}$ is the position vector of the point $\text{M}(x_1, y_1, z_1)$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given that the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the plane is $\text{M}(2, 1, -2)$, the vector $\mathbf{OM}$ from the origin to point $\text{M}$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathbf{OM} = 2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1 \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 2 \hat{\mathbf{k}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This vector $\mathbf{OM}$ is also normal to the plane because the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the plane defines the normal vector. Therefore, the vector $\mathbf{n}$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathbf{n} = 2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1 \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 2 \hat{\mathbf{k}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathbf{n} = \langle 2, 1, -2 \rangle $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the known $\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{OM}$ into the plane equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \overline{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \langle 2, 1, -2 \rangle = (2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1 \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \cdot (2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1 \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate the dot product on the right-hand side:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ (2 \times 2) + (1 \times 1) + (-2 \times -2) = 4 + 1 + 4 = 9 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the vector equation of the plane is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \overline{\mathbf{r}} \cdot (2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) = 9 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The correct option is <prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \overline{\mathbf{r}} \cdot (2 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) = 9 $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A monobasic weak acid dissociates $2 \%$ in its 0.002 M solution. Calculate the dissociation constant of weak acid.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Write given values</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Initial concentration of acid, $C = 0.002 \, \text{M}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Degree of dissociation, $\alpha = \dfrac{2}{100} = 0.02$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Formula for dissociation constant</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a weak acid $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_a = C \alpha^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-em>(Approximate because $\alpha$ is small, so equilibrium acid concentration ≈ $C$).</prep-em></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Calculation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ K_a = 0.002 \times (0.02)^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_a = 0.002 \times 0.0004 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_a = 8 \times 10^{-7} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The dissociation constant is  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{8 \times 10^{-7}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: B</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the value of dissociation constant of weak monoacidic base if it dissociates to $2 \%$ in 0.1 M solution?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Recall formula for dissociation constant</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>For a weak electrolyte:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_b = C \alpha^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$C$ = concentration of the base (M)  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\alpha$ = degree of dissociation  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Insert given values</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Concentration $C = 0.1 \, M$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Degree of dissociation = $2\% = 0.02$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_b = 0.1 \times (0.02)^2 $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Calculate</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (0.02)^2 = 0.0004 = 4 \times 10^{-4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_b = 0.1 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 4 \times 10^{-5} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>✅ Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_b = 4 \times 10^{-5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: B.</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A monobasic weak acid dissociates to $1.2 \%$ in its 0.01 M solution at 298 K . Calculate dissociation constant of it.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Write the data</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Weak acid concentration: $c = 0.01 \,\text{M}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Degree of dissociation: $\alpha = 1.2\% = 0.012$  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Formula for dissociation constant</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a weak monobasic acid $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_a = c \frac{\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Approximation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Since $\alpha = 0.012$, which is much less than 1,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 1 - \alpha \approx 0.988 \approx 1 $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_a \approx c \alpha^2 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Calculation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ K_a \approx (0.01)(0.012)^2 $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 0.01 \times 0.000144 = 1.44 \times 10^{-6} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{1.44 \times 10^{-6}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: B</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The negation of contrapositive of the statement $\mathrm{p} \rightarrow(\sim \mathrm{q} \wedge \mathrm{r})$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Contrapositive of the statement $\mathrm{p} \rightarrow(\sim \mathrm{q} \wedge \mathrm{r})$ is $\sim(\sim q \wedge r) \rightarrow \sim p$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\equiv(q \vee \sim \mathrm{r}) \rightarrow \sim \mathrm{p}$
...[De Morgan's law]</prep-p>
<prep-p>Negation of contrapositive of $p \rightarrow(\sim q \wedge r)$ is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \sim[(q \vee \sim r) \rightarrow \sim p] \\
& \equiv(q \vee \sim r) \wedge \sim(\sim p) \quad \ldots[\because \sim(p \rightarrow q) \equiv p \wedge \sim q] \\
& \equiv(q \vee \sim r) \wedge p
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The negation of the statement pattern $$\sim s \vee(\sim r \wedge s)$$ is equivalent to</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \sim(\sim s \vee(\sim r \wedge s)) \\
& \equiv s \wedge \sim(\sim r \wedge s) \quad ... [\text{De Morgan's law}]\\
& \equiv s \wedge(r \vee \sim s) \quad ... [\text{De Morgan's law}]\\
& \equiv(s \wedge r) \vee(s \wedge \sim s) \quad ... [\text{Distributive law}]\\
& \equiv(s \wedge r) \vee F \quad ... [\text{Complement law}]\\
& \equiv s \wedge r \quad ... [\text{Identity law}]
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The negation of the statement pattern $$p \vee(q \rightarrow \sim r)$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:

& \sim[p \vee(q \rightarrow \sim r)] \\
= & (\sim p) \wedge \sim(q \rightarrow \sim r) \\
= & \sim p \wedge(q \wedge \sim \sim r) \\
= & \sim p \wedge(q \wedge r)
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Negation of the statement $$\forall x \in R, x^2+1=0$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To find the negation of the given statement, we start by understanding the original statement:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\forall x \in R, x^2+1=0$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This statement declares that for every real number \(x\), the equation \(x^2+1=0\) holds true. The negation of a statement changes its truth value, essentially turning a universally quantified statement (one that applies to all members of a set) into an existentially quantified statement (one that applies to at least one member of the set), and vice versa. Additionally, it inverts the condition within the statement.</prep-p>
<prep-p>To negate the given statement, we apply the following steps:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>Change the universal quantifier (\(\forall\)) to an existential quantifier (\(\exists\)).</prep-li>
<prep-li>Invert the condition \(x^2+1=0\) to \(x^2+1 \neq 0\). The condition \(x^2+1=0\) being true for all \(x\) in \(R\) is the original claim, so negation requires that there's at least one \(x\) in \(R\) for which that condition doesn't hold.</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Therefore, the negation is: "There exists at least one real number \(x\) for which \(x^2+1 \neq 0\)."</prep-p>
<prep-p>This means Option B is the correct negation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\exists x \in R$$ such that $$x^2+1 \neq 0$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Options A and C introduce inequalities that were not part of the original statement and thus are incorrect. Option D repeats the original statement, which is not a negation.</prep-p>

questions.b: x $$\in$$ A $$\cap$$ B and (x $$\notin$$ A or x $$\notin$$ B)

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Water rises in a capillary tube of radius r upto ${ }^2$ height h . The mass of water in a capillary is m. The mass of water that will rise in capillary of radius $\frac{\mathrm{r}}{5}$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Formula for capillary rise</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The relation for capillary rise $h$ is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ h = \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho g r}, $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T$ = surface tension,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\theta$ = angle of contact,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\rho$ = liquid density,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$g$ = gravity,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$r$ = radius of the tube.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So, height of rise is $\propto \frac{1}{r}$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Volume and mass of liquid in the capillary</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The volume of the liquid column is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V = \pi r^2 h. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, the mass inside the capillary is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ m = \rho V = \rho \pi r^2 h. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $h = \tfrac{k}{r}$, where $k = \tfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ m = \rho \pi r^2 \cdot \frac{k}{r} = \rho \pi k r. $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Thus, mass $\; m \propto r$.</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Mass when radius changes</prep-h3>
<prep-p>If radius is changed from $r$ to $r/5$, then</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ m' = \frac{r}{5} \cdot (\text{same proportionality const.}). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ m' = \frac{m}{5}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The mass of water that will rise in the narrower capillary is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\tfrac{m}{5}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: A.</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Water rises in a capillary tube of radius ' $r$ ' up to height ' $h$ '. The mass of water in capillary is ' $m$ '. The mass of water that will rise in capillary of radius $\mathrm{r} / 3$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Rise of water in capillary tube is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{h}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{rpg}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For water, $\cos \theta=1$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Also, the radius of capillary tube becomes (r/3).</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad \mathrm{h}^{\prime}=\frac{3 \cdot 2 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{rgg}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~h}^{\prime}=3 \mathrm{~h}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, $m=\pi r^2 \mathrm{~h} \times \rho$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad \mathrm{m}^{\prime}=\pi(\mathrm{r} / 3)^2(3 \mathrm{~h}) \times \rho=\frac{\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~h} \rho}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{3}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Water rises in a capillary tube of radius '$$r$$' upto a height '$$h$$'. The mass of water in a capillary is '$$m$$'. The mass of water that will rise in a capillary tube of radius $$\frac{'r'}{3}$$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The rise of water in a capillary tube is due to capillary action, which is described by the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ h = \frac{2T \cos \theta}{\rho g r} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ h $ is the height of the liquid column,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ T $ is the surface tension of the liquid,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ \theta $ is the contact angle,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ \rho $ is the density of the liquid,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ g $ is the acceleration due to gravity, and</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ r $ is the radius of the capillary tube.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>When water rises in the capillary, the volume of water raised is given by the volume of the cylinder:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V = \pi r^2 h $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The mass of water in the tube is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ m = \rho V = \rho (\pi r^2 h) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the expression for $ h $ into this equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ m = \rho \left(\pi r^2 \frac{2T \cos \theta}{\rho g r}\right) = \frac{2 \pi T \cos \theta r}{g} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, for another capillary tube with radius $ \frac{r}{3} $, the corresponding mass $ m' $ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ m' = \frac{2 \pi T \cos \theta \left(\frac{r}{3}\right)}{g} = \frac{2 \pi T \cos \theta r}{3g} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the ratio of the new mass $ m' $ to the original mass $ m $ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{m'}{m} = \frac{\frac{2 \pi T \cos \theta r}{3g}}{\frac{2 \pi T \cos \theta r}{g}} = \frac{1}{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the mass of water that will rise in the capillary tube of radius $ \frac{r}{3} $ is $ \frac{m}{3} $.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>: $\frac{\mathrm{m}}{3}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Water rises in a capillary tube of radius '$$r$$' up to a height '$$\mathrm{h}$$'. The mass of water in a capillary is '$$\mathrm{m}$$'. The mass of water that will rise in a capillary tube of radius $$\frac{'r'}{3}$$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The phenomenon of capillary rise is driven by surface tension, and the height to which the liquid rises in a capillary tube is given by the Jurin's Law. The formula to determine the height of water rise in a capillary tube is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{h} = \frac{2 \gamma \cos \theta}{\rho g r}$$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>$$\gamma$$ is the surface tension of water.</prep-li>

<prep-li>$$\theta$$ is the contact angle.</prep-li>

<prep-li>$$\rho$$ is the density of water.</prep-li>

<prep-li>$$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity.</prep-li>

<prep-li>$$r$$ is the radius of the capillary tube.</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>From the above formula, it is evident that the height '$$h$$' is inversely proportional to the radius '$$r$$'.</prep-p>

<prep-p>If the radius of the capillary tube is reduced to $$\frac{r}{3}$$, the new height '$$h'$$' of water rise will be:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$h' = \frac{2 \gamma \cos \theta}{\rho g \left(\frac{r}{3}\right)} = 3 \times \frac{2 \gamma \cos \theta}{\rho g r} = 3h$$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>The mass of water in a capillary tube of radius '$$r$$' up to height '$$h$$' is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{m} = \rho \times (\text{Volume of water}) = \rho \times (\pi r^2 h)$$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Substituting height $$h'$$ and radius $$\frac{r}{3}$$ into the new volume, the new volume $$V'$$ will be:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$V' = \pi \left(\frac{r}{3}\right)^2 \times 3h = \pi \frac{r^2}{9} \times 3h = \pi \frac{r^2 h}{3}$$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus, the new mass $$m'$$ will be:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{m'} = \rho \times V' = \rho \times \pi \frac{r^2 h}{3} = \frac{\mathrm{m}}{3}$$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the mass of water that will rise in a capillary tube of radius $$\frac{r}{3}$$ is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: $$\frac{\mathrm{m}}{3}$$</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Water rises in a capillary tube of radius $$r$$ upto a height $$h$$. The mass of water in a capillary is $$m$$. The mass of water that will rise in a capillary of radius $$\frac{r}{4}$$ will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The height of water column in a capillary tube is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$h=\frac{2 \pi \cos \theta}{\rho r g}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Rightarrow \quad h \propto \frac{1}{r} \quad \text{.... (i)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Also, mass of liquid in a column of radius $r$ and height $$h$$, is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& m=\left(\pi r^2 h\right) \rho \\
& m \propto r^2 h \quad \text{.... (ii)}

<prep-p>From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get</prep-p>

& m \propto r \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \frac{m^{\prime}}{m}=\frac{\frac{r}{4}}{r} \Rightarrow m^{\prime}=\frac{m}{4}

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Distance between the parallel lines $\frac{x}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z}{1}$ and $\frac{x+4}{3}=\frac{y-3}{-2}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The vector equations of the given lines are $\bar{r}=\hat{j}+\lambda(3 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k})$ and $$\overline{\mathrm{r}}=-4 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}+\mu(3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}})$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The distance between the parallel lines $\bar{r}=\bar{a}_1+\lambda \bar{b}$ and $\bar{r}=\bar{a}_2+\mu \bar{b}$ is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$d=\left|\frac{\left(\bar{a}_2-\bar{a}_1\right) \times \bar{b}}{|\bar{b}|}\right|$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, $\bar{a}_1=\hat{j}, \bar{a}_2=-4 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}-2 \hat{k}, \bar{b}=3 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \overline{\mathrm{a}}_2-\overline{\mathrm{a}}_1=-4 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\
& \left(\bar{a}_2-\bar{a}_1\right) \times \bar{b}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\
-4 & 2 & -2 \\
3 & -2 & 1
\end{array}\right| \\
& =-2 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k} \\
& |\bar{b}|=\sqrt{9+4+1}=\sqrt{14} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{~d}=\left|\frac{-2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}}{\sqrt{14}}\right| \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{4+4+4}{14}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{12}{14}}=\sqrt{\frac{6}{7}} \text { units }
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The shortest distance between the lines $$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$$ and $$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-4}{4}=\frac{z-5}{5}$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The lines arě</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4} \text { and } \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-4}{4}=\frac{z-5}{5}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Comparing equations with</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{x-x_1}{\mathrm{a}_1}=\frac{y-y_1}{\mathrm{~b}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{z}-\mathrm{z}_1}{\mathrm{c}_1} \text { and } \frac{x-x_2}{\mathrm{a}_2}=\frac{y-y_2}{\mathrm{~b}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{z}-\mathrm{z}_2}{\mathrm{c}_2} \text {, }$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { we get } \\
& x_1=1, y_1=2, \mathrm{z}_1=3 \quad x_2=2, y_2=4, \mathrm{z}_2=5 \\
& \mathrm{a}_1=2, \mathrm{~b}_1=3, \mathrm{c}_1=4 \quad \mathrm{a}_2=3, \mathrm{~b}_2=4, \mathrm{c}_2=5 \\
& \left|\begin{array}{ccc}
x_2-x_1 \cdot & y_2-y_1 & \mathrm{z}_2-\mathrm{z}_1 \\
\mathrm{a}_1 & \mathrm{~b}_1 & \mathrm{c}_1 \\
\mathrm{a}_2 & \mathrm{~b}_2 & \mathrm{c}_2
\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 2 & 2 \\
2 & 3 & 4 \\
3 & 4 & 5
\end{array}\right| \\
& =1(15-16)-2(10-12)+2(8-9) \\
& =1 \\
& \therefore \quad \sqrt{\left(a_1 b_2-a_2 b_1\right)^2+\left(b_1 c_2-b_2 c_1\right)^2+\left(c_1 a_2-c_2 a_1\right)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{(2 \times 4-3 \times 3)^2+(3 \times 5-4 \times 4)^2+(4 \times 3-5 \times 2)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{1+1+4} \\
& =\sqrt{6} \\
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Shortest distance between line is $$\mathrm{d}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{d} & =\frac{\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
x_2-x_1 & y_2-y_1 & z_2-z_1 \\
a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\
a_2 & b_2 & c_2
\end{array}\right|}{\sqrt{\left(a_1 b_2-a_2 b_1\right)^2+\left(b_1 c_2-b_2 c_1\right)^2+\sqrt{\left(c_1 a_2-c_2 a_1\right)^2}}} \\
& =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& L_1: \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{-2}=\frac{z-3}{1} \\
& L_2=\frac{x-0}{2}=\frac{y-0}{-2}=\frac{z-0}{1}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore$$ their vector equations are</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \bar{r}=\bar{a}_1+m \bar{b} \text { and } \bar{r}=\bar{a}_2+n \bar{b}, \text { where } \\
& \bar{a}_1 \equiv(1,2,3), \bar{a}_2 \equiv(0,0,0), \bar{b} \equiv(2,-2,1)
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore\left(\bar{a}_1-\bar{a}_2\right) \times \bar{b}=\left|\begin{array}{rrr}
\hat{\boldsymbol{i}} & \hat{\boldsymbol{j}} & \hat{\boldsymbol{k}} \\
-1 & -2 & -3 \\
2 & -2 & 1
\end{array}\right| \equiv(-8,-5,6) \\
& \therefore\left|\left(\bar{a}_2-\bar{a}_1\right) \times \bar{b}\right|=\sqrt{64+25+36}=5 \sqrt{5} \\
& \quad|\bar{b}|=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3 \\
& \therefore \mathrm{d}\left(L_1, L_2\right)=\left|\frac{\left(\bar{a}_2-\bar{a}_1\right) \times \bar{b}}{b}\right|=\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{3}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is half life of a first order reaction if time required to decrease concentration of reactant from 0.4 M to 0.1 M is $x$ hour?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: General formula for first-order kinetics</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a first-order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{[a]}{[a-x]} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>or equivalently,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \ln \frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = k t $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Information given</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Initial concentration $[A]_0 = 0.4 \,M$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Final concentration $[A] = 0.1 \,M$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Time taken = $x$ hours  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ k = \frac{1}{x}\ln\frac{0.4}{0.1} = \frac{1}{x}\ln(4) = \frac{1}{x} \cdot (1.386) = \frac{1.386}{x} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Half-life for a first-order reaction</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute value of $k$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{1.386/x}  = \frac{0.693 \cdot x}{1.386} = \frac{x}{2} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The half-life of the reaction is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\tfrac{x}{2} \, \text{hour}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: C</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Rate constant of a reaction,

$$
2 \mathrm{NO}_2 \mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>is 4.7672 minute $^{-1}$. Calculate half life of reaction.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a first-order reaction, the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) is independent of the initial concentration and can be calculated using the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln(2)}{k} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$k$ is the rate constant of the reaction,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$\ln(2)$ is the natural logarithm of 2, approximately 0.693.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Rate constant, $k = 4.7672 \, \text{minute}^{-1}$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Plugging in the values, we find:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{4.7672} \approx 0.1454 \, \text{minutes} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the half-life of the reaction is <prep-strong>0.1454 minutes</prep-strong>. Thus, the correct answer is <prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Rate of a first order reaction is $1.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ minute ${ }^{-1}$ at 0.5 M concentration of reactant, calculate half life of reaction.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a first-order reaction, the rate of the reaction is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Rate} = k[A] $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $ k $ is the rate constant, and $[A]$ is the concentration of the reactant.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given the rate:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 1.5 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{mol \, L^{-1} \, min^{-1}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>and the concentration $[A] = 0.5 \, \mathrm{M}$, we can solve for the rate constant $ k $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ k = \frac{\text{Rate}}{[A]} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-2}}{0.5} = 3.0 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{min^{-1}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a first-order reaction, the half-life $(t_{1/2})$ is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the value of $ k $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{3.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 23.1 \, \text{minutes} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the correct option is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: 23.1 minute</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In a first order reaction if concentartion of reactant drops from $0.8 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ to $0.4 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ in 15 minute. What is the time required to drop concentration from $0.1 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ to 0.025 mol $\mathrm{L}^{-1}$.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>As the concentration of reactant is reduced to half i.e., from $0.8 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ to $0.4 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ in 15 minutes,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad \mathrm{t}_{1 / 2}=15$ minutes</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-img src="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/fly/@width/image/jaoe38c1m3vwwug5/bf287712-9268-4e9a-a650-1eaf19f7d7b0/0f699e40-aa8f-11ef-b7ad-813c9b426829/file-jaoe38c1m3vwwug6.png?format=png" data-orsrc="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/image/jaoe38c1m3vwwug5/bf287712-9268-4e9a-a650-1eaf19f7d7b0/0f699e40-aa8f-11ef-b7ad-813c9b426829/file-jaoe38c1m3vwwug6.png" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2024 2nd May Evening Shift Chemistry - Chemical Kinetics Question 88 English Explanation"></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \text { Time required to drop the concentration from } \\
& 0.1 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \text { to } 0.025 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}=2 \times \mathrm{t}_{1 / 2} \\
&=2 \times 15 \text { minutes } \\

questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{t}=10$$ hour, $$[\mathrm{A}]_0=1.0 \mathrm{M},[\mathrm{A}]_{\mathrm{t}}=0.25 \mathrm{M}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first order reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>(i) $$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{k} & =\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{t}} \log _{10} \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~A}]_{\mathrm{t}}} & =\frac{2.303}{10 \mathrm{~h}} \log _{10} \frac{1.0}{0.25} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{10 \mathrm{~h}} \log _{10} 4 & =\frac{2.303 \times 0.6020}{10 \mathrm{~h}} \\
& =0.139 \mathrm{~h}^{-1} &
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>(ii) $$\begin{aligned}
t_{1 / 2} & =\frac{0.693}{k} & =\frac{0.693}{0.139 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}} \\

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an ionic crystalline solid, atoms of element Y forms hcp structure. The atoms of element X occupy one third of tetrahedral voids. What is the formula of compound?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the formula of the compound, we need to understand the relationships between the number of atoms (or ions) in the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure and the number of tetrahedral voids available, along with how many of these voids are occupied by the atoms of element X.</prep-p>

<prep-p>In a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure, each atom of element Y contributes to the close-packed structure. For convenience, we can assume that there are 6 atoms of Y in the hcp arrangement. The reason for choosing 6 is because it's a multiple that simplifies calculations in the hcp lattice where each atom is surrounded by 12 others, but each atom itself is shared among multiple unit cells. Nonetheless, the exact number chosen for Y is irrelevant to the ratio we are trying to calculate, as the ratio of tetrahedral voids to atoms in an hcp structure remains constant regardless of the number of atoms considered.</prep-p>

<prep-p>In a close-packed structure, the number of tetrahedral voids is twice the number of atoms present. Thus, if we have 6 Y atoms in the hcp structure, we have $$2 \times 6 = 12$$ tetrahedral voids.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Given that atoms of element X occupy one-third of the tetrahedral voids, the number of X atoms occupying the tetrahedral voids is $$\frac{1}{3} \times 12 = 4.$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus, we have 6 Y atoms and 4 X atoms. To find the simplest whole number ratio, we divide by the smallest number of atoms present among the elements, which gives us:</prep-p>

<prep-p>For Y: $$\frac{6}{2} = 3$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>For X: $$\frac{4}{2} = 2$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>This results in a formula of $$\mathrm{X}_2\mathrm{Y}_3$$, indicating that the correct answer is Option A.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the number of octahedral and tetrahedral voids presents respectively in 0.25 mole of a substance having hcp structure?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>In a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure, each atom contributes to the formation of both octahedral and tetrahedral voids. To find the number of these voids, we can follow these steps:</prep-p>

<prep-p>1. Determine the total number of atoms in 0.25 moles of the given substance.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The number of atoms in one mole of a substance is Avogadro's number, $$N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$$. Therefore, the number of atoms in 0.25 mole is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 0.25 \times N_A = 0.25 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.5055 \times 10^{23} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>2. In an hcp structure, the number of octahedral voids per atom is equal to the number of atoms. So, the number of octahedral voids in 0.25 moles of the substance is also:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 1.5055 \times 10^{23} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>3. The number of tetrahedral voids per atom in a close-packed structure is twice the number of atoms. So, the number of tetrahedral voids in 0.25 moles of the substance is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 2 \times 1.5055 \times 10^{23} = 3.011 \times 10^{23} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Hence, the number of octahedral and tetrahedral voids present respectively in 0.25 mole of a substance having hcp structure are:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 1.5055 \times 10^{23}, 3.011 \times 10^{23} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the correct option is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option D</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ 1.50 \times 10^{23}, 3.011 \times 10^{23} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the number of unit cells in 0.79 g metal if product of density and volume of unit cell is $1.58 \times 10^{-22} \mathrm{~g}$.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Mass of the metal sample = $0.79 \, \text{g}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Product of density and volume of unit cell = $1.58 \times 10^{-22} \, \text{g}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Understanding the given product</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{Density} \times \text{Volume of unit cell} = \text{Mass of one unit cell} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Mass of one unit cell} = 1.58 \times 10^{-22} \, \text{g} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Number of unit cells in the sample</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{Number of unit cells} = \frac{\text{Total mass of sample}}{\text{Mass of one unit cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{0.79}{1.58 \times 10^{-22}} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Calculate</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \frac{0.79}{1.58} = 0.5 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Number of unit cells} = 0.5 \times 10^{22} = 5.0 \times 10^{21} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: $5.0 \times 10^{21}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the number of unit cells in $1 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ volume of an element if unit cell edge length is $4.0 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~cm}$.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Volume of sample, $V = 1~\mathrm{cm}^3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Edge length of unit cell, $a = 4.0 \times 10^{-8}~\mathrm{cm}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Calculate volume of one unit cell</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Volume of one unit cell} = a^3 = (4.0 \times 10^{-8}~\mathrm{cm})^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 4.0^3 \times (10^{-8})^3~\mathrm{cm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 64 \times 10^{-24}~\mathrm{cm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 6.4 \times 10^{-23}~\mathrm{cm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Calculate number of unit cells</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Number of unit cells} = \frac{\text{Total volume of sample}}{\text{Volume of one unit cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{1~\mathrm{cm}^3}{6.4 \times 10^{-23}~\mathrm{cm}^3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{1}{6.4} \times 10^{23} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 0.15625 \times 10^{23} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 1.5625 \times 10^{22} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Choose the correct option</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Rounding to three significant figures, the answer is:</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the number of unit cells in 0.9 g metal if it forms bec structure. $\left[\rho \times \mathrm{a}^3=3 \times 10^{-22}\right.$ gram$]$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>In order to calculate the number of unit cells for a metal forming a Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) structure in 0.9 grams, we start with the following information:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>The density-volume relationship is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \rho \times a^3 = 3 \times 10^{-22} \, \text{grams} $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>The weight of the metal: 0.9 grams.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>A BCC unit cell contains 2 atoms per unit cell.</prep-p>
<prep-p>To determine the number of unit cells, follow these steps:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>Calculate the mass of one unit cell:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Mass of one unit cell} = \rho \times a^3 = 3 \times 10^{-22} \, \text{grams} $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Calculate the number of unit cells in 0.9 grams of the metal by dividing the total mass by the mass of one unit cell:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$     \text{Number of unit cells} = \frac{\text{Total mass}}{\text{Mass of one unit cell}} = \frac{0.9 \, \text{grams}}{3 \times 10^{-22} \, \text{grams}}     $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Simplify the calculation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    \text{Number of unit cells} = \frac{0.9}{3 \times 10^{-22}} = \frac{0.9 \times 10^{22}}{3} = 0.3 \times 10^{22}    $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Convert this to a more standard scientific notation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 0.3 \times 10^{22} = 3.0 \times 10^{21} $$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus, option C is correct, with the number of unit cells being:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 3.0 \times 10^{21} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The value of $\int \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{x^2\left(x^4+1\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}}$ is</prep-p>
questions.b: $\left(x^4+1\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}+\mathrm{c}$, where c is constant of integration.
questions.c: $-\left(x^4+1\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}+\mathrm{c}$, where c is constant of integration.
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { Let } \mathrm{I} & =\int \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{x^2\left(x^4+1\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}} \\
& =\int \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{x^2 \times x^3\left(\frac{x^4+1}{x^4}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}} \\
& =\int \frac{1}{x^5}\left(\frac{x^4+1}{x^4}\right)^{\frac{-3}{4}} \mathrm{~d} x
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Let } \frac{x^4+1}{x^4}=t \\
& \text { i.e., } 1+\frac{1}{x^4}=t \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{-4}{x^5} d x=d t
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad I & =\frac{-1}{4} \int t^{\frac{-3}{4}} d t \\
& =-t^{\frac{1}{4}}+c \\
& =-\left(\frac{x^4+1}{x^4}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}+c
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an a.c. circuit, a resistance ' $R$ ' is connected in series with an inductance ' $L$ '. If phase angle between voltage and current is $45^{\circ}$, the value of inductive reactance will be $\left(\tan 45^{\circ}=1\right)$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Relation between phase angle and reactance</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a series $RL$ circuit, the phase angle $\phi$ between voltage and current is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $X_L = \omega L$ = inductive reactance.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Apply the given data</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \phi = 45^{\circ}, \quad \tan 45^\circ = 1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = 1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \implies X_L = R $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The value of inductive reactance is <prep-strong>$R$</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: A (R)</prep-strong> ✅</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>With an alternating voltage source frequency ' f ', inductor ' $L$ ', capacitor ' $C$ ' and resistance ' $R$ ' are connected in series. The voltage leads the current by $45^{\circ}$. The value of ' $L$ ' is $\left(\tan 45^{\circ}=1\right)$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The phase difference between the current and
the voltage is given by $\tan \phi=\frac{\omega \mathrm{L}-\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}}}{\mathrm{R}}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \omega \mathrm{L}-\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{R} \quad \ldots\left(\because \tan \phi=\tan 45^{\circ}=1\right) \\
\therefore & \omega \mathrm{L}=\mathrm{R}+\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}} \\
\therefore & \mathrm{~L}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\omega}+\frac{1}{\omega^2 \mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mathrm{R} \omega \mathrm{C}+1}{\omega^2 \mathrm{C}} \\
\therefore & \mathrm{~L}=\frac{1+2 \pi \mathrm{fCR}}{4 \pi^2 \mathrm{f}^2 \mathrm{C}} \quad \ldots .(\because \omega=2 \pi \mathrm{f})
\end{array}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>With an alternating voltage source of frequency '$$f$$', inductor '$$L$$', capacitor '$$C$$' and resistance '$$R$$' are connected in series. The voltage leads the current by $$45^{\circ}$$. The value of '$$L$$' is $$\left(\tan 45^{\circ}=1\right)$$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \tan \phi=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R} \\
& \Rightarrow \tan 45^{\circ}=\left[\frac{2 \pi f L-\frac{1}{2 \pi f C}}{R}\right] \quad \ldots .\left(\because \phi=45^{\circ}\right) \\
& R=\frac{(2 \pi f)^2 L C-1}{2 \pi f C} \\
& \therefore \quad L=\frac{2 \pi f \mathrm{CR}+1}{4 \pi^2 \mathrm{f}^2 \mathrm{C}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an a.c. circuit, a resistance R = 40 $$\Omega$$ and an inductance 'L' are connected in series. If the phase angle between voltage and current is 45$$^\circ$$, then the value of the inductive reactance is (tan 45$$^\circ$$ = 1)</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>In an AC circuit where a resistance $ R = 40 \ \Omega $ and an inductance $ L $ are connected in series, the phase angle $ \phi $ between the voltage and current is given as 45$$^\circ$$. We need to determine the inductive reactance $ X_L $.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The phase angle in an RL series circuit is given by the tangent of the angle:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \tan(\phi) = \frac{X_L}{R} $$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Given $ \phi = 45^\circ $ and $ \tan 45^\circ = 1 $, we have:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \tan(45^\circ) = \frac{X_L}{R} = 1 $$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ X_L = R $$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Given $ R = 40 \ \Omega $, we find:</prep-p>

<prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ X_L = 40 \ \Omega $$</prep-p>

</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the value of the inductive reactance is 40$$\Omega$$ (Option B).</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The population of towns A and B increase at the rate proportional to their population present at that time. At the end of the year 1984, the population of both the towns was 20,000 . At the end of the year 1989, the population of town A was 25,000 and that of town B was 28,000 . The difference of populations of towns A and B at the end of 1994 was</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}$ be the populations of town A and town $B$ at time $t$ years, respectively.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Then, $\frac{d P_A}{d t}=k_1 P_A$ and $\frac{d P_B}{d t}=k_2 P_B$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dP}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}}=\mathrm{k}_1 \mathrm{dt}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{dP}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\mathrm{k}_2 \mathrm{dt}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Integrating on both sides, we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\log P_A=k_1 t+c_1$ and</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\log \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{k}_2 \mathrm{t}+\mathrm{c}_2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}=20,000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore \quad & \log 20000=\mathrm{c}_1 \text { and } \\ \therefore \quad & \log 20000=\mathrm{c}_2 \\ & \log \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{k}_1 \mathrm{t}+\log 20000 \text { and } \\ & \log \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{k}_2 \mathrm{t}+\log 20000 \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}}{20000}\right)=\mathrm{k}_1 \mathrm{t} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(i)\\ & \text { and } \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}}{20000}\right)=\mathrm{k}_2 \mathrm{t} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(ii)\end{array} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Town A:</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=1989-1984=5, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}=25,000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \therefore \quad \log \left(\frac{25000}{20000}\right)=5 \mathrm{k}_1 $$         …[From (i)]</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow k_1=\frac{1}{5} \log \left(\frac{5}{4}\right) \\ \therefore \quad & \log \left(\frac{P_A}{20000}\right)=\frac{t}{5} \log \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)\,\,\,\, …[From (i)] \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \text { When } t=1994-1984=10 \\ & \log \left(\frac{P_A}{20000}\right)=\frac{10}{5} \log \left(\frac{5}{4}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{P_A}{20000}\right)=2 \log \left(\frac{5}{4}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{P_A}{20000}=\frac{25}{16} \\ & \Rightarrow P_A=31,250 \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Town B:</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=1989-1984=5, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}=28,000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \therefore \quad \log \left(\frac{28000}{20000}\right)=5 \mathrm{k}_2\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,. . .[\text { From (ii)] } $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}_2=\frac{1}{5} \log \left(\frac{7}{5}\right) \\ \therefore & \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}}}{20000}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{t}}{5} \log \left(\frac{7}{5}\right) \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,. . .[\text { From (ii)] }\end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \text { When } t=1994-1984=10 \\ & \log \left(\frac{P_B}{20000}\right)=\frac{10}{5} \log \left(\frac{7}{5}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{P_B}{20000}\right)=2 \log \left(\frac{7}{5}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{P_B}{20000}=\frac{49}{25} \\ & \Rightarrow P_B=39,200 \end{aligned}\\ &\therefore \quad \text { Difference of populations }\\ &=39200-31250=7950 \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The rate at which the population of a city increases varies as the population. In a period of 20 years, the population increased from 4 lakhs to 6 lakhs. In another 20 years the population will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let P be the population at time t years.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Then, $\frac{\mathrm{dP}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\mathrm{kP}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dP}}{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{kdt} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Integrating on both sides, we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log P=k t+c $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{P}=400000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \log 400000=0+\mathrm{c} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{c}=\log 400000 \\ \therefore & \log \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{kt}+\log 400000 \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}}{400000}\right)=\mathrm{kt} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(i)\end{array} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $t=20$ years, $P=600000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore \quad & \log \left(\frac{600000}{400000}\right)=20 \mathrm{k} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}=\frac{1}{20} \log \left(\frac{3}{2}\right) \\ \therefore \quad & \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}}{400000}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{t}}{20} \log \frac{3}{2} \,\,\,\,\, ... [From (i)] \end{array} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ Population after another 20 years i.e. $\mathrm{t}=40$ years,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}}{400000}\right)=\frac{40}{20} \log \frac{3}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}}{400000}\right)=2 \log \frac{3}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{P}}{400000}=\frac{9}{4} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}=9 \text { lakhs } \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The population of a town increases at a rate proportional to the population at that time. If the population increases from forty thousand to eighty thousand in 20 years, then the population in another 40 years will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let P be the population at time t years.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{d p}{d t} \propto P $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Then, $\frac{\mathrm{dP}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\mathrm{kP}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dP}}{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{kdt} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Integrating on both sides, we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{kt}+\mathrm{c} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{P}=40000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \log 40000=0+\mathrm{c} \Rightarrow \mathrm{c}=\log 40000 \\ \therefore & \log \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{kt}+\log 40000 \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}}{40000}\right)=\mathrm{kt} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(i)\end{array} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=20 \mathrm{yrs}, \mathrm{P}=80000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad & \log \left(\frac{80000}{40000}\right)=20 \mathrm{k} \\ & \Rightarrow \log 2=20 \mathrm{k} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}=\frac{\log 2}{20} \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{P}}{40000}\right)=\frac{\log 2}{20} \mathrm{t}   \,\,\,\,\,\,\,    …[From (i)]\end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\text { Population in another } 40 \text { years }\\ &\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \text { When, } t=60 \\ & \log \left(\frac{P}{40000}\right)=\frac{\log 2}{20} \times 60 \\ & \log \left(\frac{P}{40000}\right)=3 \log 2 \\ & \frac{P}{40000}=8 \\ & P=3,20,000 \end{array} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The population of a town increases at a rate proportional to the population at that time. If the population increases from 40 thousand to 80 thousand in 40 years, then the population in another 40 years will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let p be the population at time $t$ years.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Then } \frac{d p}{d t}=k p \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{d p}{p}=k d t
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Integrating on both sides, we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\log \mathrm{p}=\mathrm{kt}+\mathrm{c}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>when $t=0, p=40000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \log 40000=0+c \\
& \quad \Rightarrow c=\log 40000
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & \log \mathrm{p}=\mathrm{kt}+\log 40000 \\
& \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{p}}{40000}\right)=\mathrm{kt}\quad\text{.... (i)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $\mathrm{t}=40$ years, $\mathrm{p}=80000$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{80000}{40000}\right)=40 \mathrm{k} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}=\frac{1}{40} \log 2 \\
\therefore \quad & \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{p}}{40000}\right)=\frac{1}{40} \log 2 \times \mathrm{t}\quad\text{.... [From (i)]}

& \Rightarrow p=16,0000
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Let the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-5}=\frac{z+2}{2}$ lie in the plane $x+3 y-\alpha z+\beta=0$, then the value of $(\beta-\alpha)$ is equal to</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We are asked:</prep-p>
<prep-blockquote>
  <prep-p>Let the line  </prep-p>
  <prep-p>$ > \frac{x-2}{3} \;=\; \frac{y-1}{-5} \;=\; \frac{z+2}{2} > $</prep-p>
  <prep-p>lie in the plane  </prep-p>
  <prep-p>$ > x + 3y - \alpha z + \beta = 0, > $  </prep-p>
  <prep-p>then find $(\beta - \alpha)$.</prep-p>
</prep-blockquote>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Write parametric form of line</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Let the parameter be $t$. Then:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x = 2 + 3t, \quad y = 1 - 5t, \quad z = -2 + 2t. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So point on the line when $t=0$ is $P(2,1,-2)$. The direction vector of line is $(3,-5,2)$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Condition for line to lie in plane</prep-h3>
<prep-p>If the entire line lies in the plane, then:</prep-p>
<prep-ol>
<prep-li><prep-p>The <prep-strong>direction vector</prep-strong> of the line must be parallel to the plane (so its dot product with plane's normal is zero).</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>One point on the line must satisfy the plane equation.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ol>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Normal vector of plane: $(1,3,-\alpha)$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Direction vector of line: $(3,-5,2)$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So condition:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (1,3,-\alpha)\cdot(3,-5,2) = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Compute:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 3 + (3)(-5) + (-\alpha)(2) = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 3 - 15 - 2\alpha = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; -12 - 2\alpha = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \alpha = -6. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Substitute point into plane</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Equation of plane:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x + 3y - \alpha z + \beta = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>With $\alpha = -6$, equation is  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x + 3y -(-6)z + \beta = x + 3y + 6z + \beta = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Point $P(2,1,-2)$ lies on it, so:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2 + 3(1) + 6(-2) + \beta = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2 + 3 - 12 + \beta = 0. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ -7 + \beta = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \beta = 7. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Find $\beta - \alpha$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \beta - \alpha = 7 - (-6) = 13. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{13} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: B.</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>If the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-5}=\frac{z+2}{2}$ lies in the plane $x+3 y-\alpha z+\beta=0$, then $(\alpha, \beta)=$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The line $$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-5}=\frac{z+2}{2}$$ lies in the plane $$x+3 y-\alpha z+\beta=0$$, then the value of $$\alpha^2+\alpha \beta+\beta^2$$ is</prep-p>

<prep-p>Line $$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-5}=\frac{z+2}{2}$$ lies in the plane $$x+3 y-\alpha z+\beta=0$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The direction ratios of the line are $$3,-5,2$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The direction ratios of the normal to the plane are $$1,3,-\alpha$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The given line is perpendicular to the normal of plane.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & 3(1)+(-5)(3)+2(-\alpha)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 3-15-2 \alpha=0 \\
& \Rightarrow-12-2 \alpha=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \alpha=-6
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Also, point $$(2,1,-2)$$ lies on the plane</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}

& \Rightarrow 2+3-(-6)(-2)+\beta=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 2+3-12+\beta=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \beta=7 \\
\therefore \quad & \alpha^2+\alpha \beta+\beta^2=36-42+49=43
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The line $$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-5}=\frac{z+2}{2}$$ lies in the plane $$x+3 y-\alpha z+\beta=0$$, then value of $$\alpha \beta$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:

\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The ratio of energies of photons produced due to transition of electron of hydrogen atom from its (i) third to $2^{\text {nd }}$ energy level and (ii) highest energy level to $3^{\text {rd }}$ level is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-strong>Case (i):</prep-strong> Electron transition from $n=3 \to n=2$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Photon energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{n_2^2} - \frac{1}{n_1^2}\right)\ \text{eV}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E_{(3 \to 2)} = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \left(\frac{9 - 4}{36}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \cdot \frac{5}{36}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{68}{36} = \frac{17}{9}\ \text{eV}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Case (ii):</prep-strong> Transition from highest energy level ($n = \infty$) to $n=3$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Energy of photon:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \cdot \frac{1}{9}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{13.6}{9} = \frac{136}{90} = \frac{68}{45}\ \text{eV}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Now ratio:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{E_{(3 \to 2)}}{E_{(\infty \to 3)}} = \frac{\tfrac{17}{9}}{\tfrac{68}{45}}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{17}{9} \cdot \frac{45}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{17 \cdot 45}{9 \cdot 68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{17 \cdot 5}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{85}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{85}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide numerator and denominator by 17:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{5}{4}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{5:4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>That matches <prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>. ✅</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The ratio of energies of photons produced due to transition of electron of hydrogen atom from its (i) second to first energy level and (ii) highest energy level to second level is respectively</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The energy of photons is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$E=R h c\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where, $$R$$ is Rydberg constant, $$h$$ is Planck's constant and $$c$$ is the speed of light.</prep-p>
<prep-p>(i) Energy of photon produced from second to first energy level,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& E_1=R h c\left(\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}\right) \\
& E_1=\frac{3}{4} R h c
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>(ii) Energy of photon produced from highest energy level (i.e., $$\infty$$) to second level,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& E_2=R h c\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\frac{1}{4} R h c \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{\frac{3}{4} R h c}{\frac{1}{4} R h c}=\frac{3}{1} \text { or } 3: 1
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A monoatomic ideal gas, initially at temperature $\mathrm{T}_1$ is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with massless, frictionless piston. By releasing the piston suddenly, the gas is allowed to expand adiabatically to a temperature $\mathrm{T}_2$. If $\mathrm{L}_1$ and $\mathrm{L}_2$ are the lengths of the gas columns before and after expansion respectively, then $\left(T_2 / T_1\right)$ is given by</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Adiabatic process formula:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>For an adiabatic process, the following formula holds:<prep-br>

$$ \mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}= \text{constant} $$

This means:<prep-br>

$$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1} $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Value of $\gamma$ for monoatomic gas:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>For a monoatomic gas, $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Calculate $\gamma-1$:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

$\gamma - 1 = \frac{5}{3} - 1 = \frac{2}{3}$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Relating volume to length:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

The volume of gas is calculated as the area ($A$) of the cylinder times the length ($L$) of the gas column.<prep-br>

So, $\mathrm{V}_1 = \mathrm{A} \mathrm{L}_1$ and $\mathrm{V}_2 = \mathrm{A} \mathrm{L}_2$.

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Substitute in the temperature formula:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

Now, substitute these volumes into the earlier formula:<prep-br>

$$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left(\frac{\mathrm{A} \mathrm{L}_1}{\mathrm{A} \mathrm{L}_2}\right)^{2/3} $$

The area ($A$) cancels out:

$$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_1}{\mathrm{L}_2}\right)^{2/3} $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Final result:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

So, the ratio of the final and initial temperature is:<prep-br>

$$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left( \frac{\mathrm{L}_1}{\mathrm{L}_2} \right)^{2/3} $$

</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A monoatomic ideal gas, initially at temperature $T_1$ is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with frictionless piston. The gas is allowed to expand adiabatically to a temperature $T_2$ by releasing the piston suddenly. $L_1$ and $L_2$ are the lengths of the gas columns before and after the expansion respectively. The ratio $T_2 / T_1$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For an adiabatic process involving an ideal gas, the relationship between initial and final states is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{V}_1^{\gamma-1} = \mathrm{T}_2 \mathrm{V}_2^{\gamma-1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>From this, the ratio of the final to initial temperatures is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a monoatomic gas, the adiabatic index $\gamma$ is $\frac{5}{3}$. Thus:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \gamma - 1 = \frac{5}{3} - 1 = \frac{2}{3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>The volume of the gas is calculated using the area of the base and the length of the gas column. Thus:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mathrm{V}_1 = \mathrm{A}L_1 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{V}_2 = \mathrm{A}L_2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>By substituting these into the expression for $\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}L_1}{\mathrm{A}L_2}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the ratio of the final to initial temperature after adiabatic expansion is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1} = \left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_1}{\mathrm{L}_2}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} $</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A monoatomic ideal gas initially at temperature '$$\mathrm{T}_1$$' is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with massless, frictionless piston. By releasing the piston suddenly the gas is allowed to expand to adiabatically to a temperature '$$\mathrm{T}_2$$'. If '$$\mathrm{L}_1$$' and '$$\mathrm{L}_2$$' are the lengths of the gas columns before and after expansion respectively, then $$\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{ll} 
& \text { For an adiabatic process } \\
& \mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2^{\gamma-1} \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}
\end{array}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a monoatomic gas, $$r=\frac{5}{3}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{cl} 
& \Rightarrow \gamma-1=\frac{5}{3}-1=\frac{2}{3} \\
& V_1=A L_1 \text { and } V_2=A L_2 \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\left[\frac{A L_1}{A L_2}\right]^{2 / 3}=\left[\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^{2 / 3} \\
& \gamma-1=\frac{2}{3}
\end{array}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For an adiabatic process,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} \\
& \mathrm{~V} \propto \mathrm{L} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_1}{\mathrm{~L}_2}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A monoatomic ideal gas initially at temperature $$\mathrm{T}_1$$ is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with 8 frictionless piston. The gas is allowed to expand adiabatically to a temperature $$\mathrm{T}_2$$ by releasing the piston suddenly. $$\mathrm{L}_1$$ and $$\mathrm{L}_2$$ are the lengths of the gas columns before and after the expansion respectively. Then $$\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For adiabatic expansion we have</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2^{\gamma-1} \\
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_1}{\mathrm{~L}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1} \quad[\because \mathrm{v} \propto \mathrm{L}] \\

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Eight small drops of mercury each of radius '$$r$$', coalesce to form a large single drop. The ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>When mercury drops coalesce to form a larger drop, the volume is conserved. The total initial volume of the eight small drops is equal to the final volume of the large single drop.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a single small drop with radius $$r$$, its volume is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_{\text{small}} = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For eight such drops, the total initial volume is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_{\text{initial}} = 8 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 = \frac{32}{3} \pi r^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let the radius of the large drop be $$R$$. Since the volume is conserved:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_{\text{large}} = \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \frac{32}{3} \pi r^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Equating the volumes:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \frac{32}{3} \pi r^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Solving for $$R$$ gives:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ R^3 = 8r^3 \implies R = 2r $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The total surface energy of the drops depends on the surface area and the surface tension ($$\sigma$$). The formula for surface energy is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Surface Energy} = \sigma \times \text{Surface Area} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The surface area of a single small drop is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ A_{\text{small}} = 4 \pi r^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The total initial surface area of the eight small drops is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ A_{\text{initial}} = 8 \times 4 \pi r^2 = 32 \pi r^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The surface area of the large drop is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ A_{\text{large}} = 4 \pi R^2 = 4 \pi (2r)^2 = 16 \pi r^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the initial total surface energy of the small drops is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{initial}} = \sigma \times 32 \pi r^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The surface energy of the large drop is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{large}} = \sigma \times 16 \pi r^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The ratio of the total surface energy before and after the amalgamation is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{E_{\text{initial}}}{E_{\text{large}}} = \frac{\sigma \times 32 \pi r^2}{\sigma \times 16 \pi r^2} = \frac{32}{16} = 2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the ratio is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>: 2 : 1</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two small drops of mercury each of radius '$$R$$' coalesce to form a large single drop. The ratio of the total surface energies before and after the change is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Total surface energy before coalesce</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{E}_1=2\left(4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2\right) \mathrm{T}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>But $$\frac{4}{3} \pi R^2 \times 2=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^{\prime 3}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Total surface energy after coalesce</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& E_2=4 \pi R^{\prime 2} T=4 \pi 2^{2 / 3} R^2 T \\
& \therefore \frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{2\left(4 \pi R^2\right) T}{4 \pi 2^{2 / 3} R^2 T}=2^{1-\frac{2}{3}}=2^{1 / 3}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two small drops of mercury each of radius $$r$$ coalesce to form a large single drop. The ratio of the total surface energies before and after the change is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The surface energy of a drop is directly proportional to its surface area. The surface area of a sphere (in this case, a mercury drop) is given by the formula $$4\pi r^2$$, where $$r$$ is the radius of the sphere. When two small drops, each of radius $$r$$, coalesce, they form a larger drop. The volume of mercury is conserved in this process. Let's perform the calculations step by step:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Calculate the volume of one small drop and the total volume of two drops.</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>The volume of a sphere is given by $$\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$. Thus, the volume of one small drop is $$\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$, and the total volume of the two small drops before coalescence is $$2\times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{8}{3}\pi r^3$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Calculate the radius of the large drop formed after coalescence.</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>Let the radius of the large drop be $$R$$. The volume of the large drop is $$\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$$. Since volume is conserved, we have:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{8}{3}\pi r^3$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Solving for $$R$$ gives:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$R^3 = 2r^3$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>So, $$R = 2^{\frac{1}{3}}r$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Calculate the ratio of the total surface energies before and after the change.</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>The surface energy is proportional to the surface area. The total surface area of the two small drops is $$2 \times 4\pi r^2 = 8\pi r^2$$, and the surface area of the large drop is $$4\pi R^2$$. Substituting $$R = 2^{\frac{1}{3}}r$$:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$4\pi R^2 = 4\pi (2^{\frac{1}{3}}r)^2 = 4\pi 2^{\frac{2}{3}}r^2$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The ratio of the total surface energies (which is proportional to the ratio of the total surface areas) before and after the change is thus:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\frac{8\pi r^2}{4\pi 2^{\frac{2}{3}}r^2} = \frac{8}{4 \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{3}}} = \frac{2}{2^{\frac{2}{3}}} = 2^{\frac{3}{3}}:2^{\frac{2}{3}} = 2:2^{\frac{2}{3}} = 2^{\frac{1}{3}}:1$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the correct option is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option B $$2^{\frac{1}{3}}: 1$$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two small drops of mercury each of radius ' $R$ ' coalesce to form a large single drop. The ratio of the total surface energies before and after the change is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given that, the two small drops of mercury
and radius $R$ of each drop coalesce to form a large drop of radius $r$, so the net volume remains constant i.e,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { initial volume } & =\text { final volume } \\
V_{\text {initial }} & =\mathrm{V}_{\text {final }} \\
2 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 & =1 \cdot \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \Rightarrow r=2^{1 / 3} R\quad \text{.... (i)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>As, surface tension is constant for both the drops.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, the surface energy of two small drops,<prep-p>
<prep-p>$$E_1=2 \times T A_1=2 \times 4 \pi R^2 \times T$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Surface energy of one big drop,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$E_2=T A_2=4 \pi r^2 \times T=2^{1 / 3} .4 \pi R^2 T \text { (using Eq. (i)) }$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Ratio the total surface energy before and after the change is given as,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{8 \pi}{2^{2 / 3}} \frac{R^2 T}{4 \pi R^2 T}=\frac{2^{1-\frac{2}{3}}}{1}=2^{\frac{1}{3}}: 1$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Hence, the ratio of surface energy of the each drop is $2^{\frac{1}{3}}: 1$.</prep-p>
