questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which among the following is a cationic complex?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The option that represents a cationic complex is <prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>, $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}\right] \mathrm{SO}_4$.</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Explanation:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>A cationic complex is a coordination compound in which the complex ion has a positive charge. Let's analyze the given options to determine which comprises a cationic complex:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>: $\mathrm{Na}_4\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>This consists of $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]^{4-}$ as the anion tetrasodium cation, making it an anionic complex.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>: $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}\right] \mathrm{SO}_4$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}\right]^+$ is the cation and $\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}$ is the anion, which means it is a cationic complex.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong>: $\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_4\right]$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>This neutral complex (having no charge) is formed by carbon monoxide Ligands which are neutral.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Option D</prep-strong>: $\mathrm{K}_3\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>This involves $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]^{3-}$ complex anion, paired with $\mathrm{K}^+$, which is an anionic complex formed by tripotassium cation.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus, Option B is the correct cationic complex.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Identify anionic sphere complex from following.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The term "anionic sphere complex" refers to a complex ion that carries a net negative charge. To identify an anionic sphere complex among the options provided, we need to look at the complex ions and see which ones are negatively charged.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option A: Hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. This complex is [Co(NH<prep-sub>3</prep-sub>)<prep-sub>6</prep-sub>]<prep-sup>3+</prep-sup> and carries a net positive charge. Therefore, it is not an anionic sphere complex.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option B: Potassium hexacyanoferrate(II). This complex is [Fe(CN)<prep-sub>6</prep-sub>]<prep-sup>4-</prep-sup>, which carries a net negative charge. Therefore, it is an anionic sphere complex.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option C: Tetraamminedichlorocobalt(III) ion. This complex ion is [Co(NH<prep-sub>3</prep-sub>)<prep-sub>4</prep-sub>Cl<prep-sub>2</prep-sub>]<prep-sup>+</prep-sup>, which carries a net positive charge. Thus, it is not an anionic sphere complex.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option D: Pentaamminechlorocobalt(III) sulphate. This complex itself is [Co(NH<prep-sub>3</prep-sub>)<prep-sub>5</prep-sub>Cl]<prep-sup>2+</prep-sup> and carries a net positive charge. So, it is not an anionic sphere complex.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The correct answer is <prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>: Potassium hexacyanoferrate(II), which features the anionic complex [Fe(CN)<prep-sub>6</prep-sub>]<prep-sup>4-</prep-sup>.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which among following complexes is a neutral complex?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The complexes in which the coordination sphere does not carry any charge are called neutral complexes.
$$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NO}_2\right)_3\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_3\right]$$ is a neutral complex. $$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5\right] \mathrm{I}_3$$ and $$\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_3(\mathrm{NCS})\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2$$ are cationic complexes whereas $$\mathrm{Na}\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NO}_2\right)_6\right]$$ is an anionic complex.</prep-p>
<prep-p>A neutral complex does not have any counter ion (either positive or negative). So, options (A), (C) and (D) can be eliminated.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: The time period of a simple pendulum inside a stationary lift is $\sqrt{3}$ second. When the lift moves upwards with an acceleration $g / 3$, the time period will be ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Time period in stationary lift, $T_1 = \sqrt{3}$ s  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Acceleration due to gravity = $g$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Lift moves upwards with acceleration $a = \frac{g}{3}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Time period formula for a simple pendulum</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>In general,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $g_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective acceleration due to gravity.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Effective gravity in the stationary case</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>When the lift is stationary, $g_{\text{eff}} = g$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_1 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Effective gravity when lift moves upward</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>When lift accelerates upwards with $a$,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ g_{\text{eff}} = g + a = g + \frac{g}{3} = \frac{4g}{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: New time period</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The new time period is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\frac{4g}{3}}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{3l}{4g}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Express $l$ in terms of $T_1$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_1 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Square both sides:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_1^2 = 4\pi^2 \frac{l}{g} \implies l = \frac{g T_1^2}{4\pi^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, substitute $l$ into $T_2$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{3}{4g} \cdot \frac{g T_1^2}{4\pi^2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{3 T_1^2}{16\pi^2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = 2\pi \cdot \frac{T_1}{4\pi} \sqrt{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = \frac{T_1}{2} \sqrt{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 5: Substitute $T_1 = \sqrt{3}$ s</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_2 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \sqrt{3} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5\ \text{seconds} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Option <prep-strong>A) 1.5 s</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In a stationary lift, time period of a simple pendulum is '$$\mathrm{T}$$'. The lift starts accelerating downwards with acceleration $$\left(\frac{\mathrm{g}}{4}\right)$$, then the time period of the pendulum will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Time period of pendulum: $$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When lift is accelerated downward with acceleration $$\frac{\mathrm{g}}{4}$$,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& g=g-\frac{g}{4} \\
& g=\frac{3 g}{4}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore\quad$$ New Time period will be</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& T_1=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{4 L}{3 g}} \\
& T_1=2 \pi \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \\
& T_1=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} T
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The time period of a simple pendulum inside a stationary lift is '$$T$$'. When the lift starts accelerating upwards with an acceleration $$\left(\frac{\mathrm{g}}{3}\right)$$, the time period of the pendulum will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Time period of a simple pendulum is $$\mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\left(\frac{l}{\mathrm{a}}\right)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>In stationary lift, the value of acceleration is $$\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{g}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\left(\frac{l}{\mathrm{~g}}\right)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When the lift is accelerating in an upward direction, there is a pseudo force acting in a downward direction.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{ma}=\mathrm{mg}+\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{3} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{g}+\frac{\mathrm{g}}{3} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{a}=\frac{4 \mathrm{~g}}{3}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad$$ Period for a pendulum in accelerating lift is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\quad \mathrm{T}^{\prime} & =2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\mathrm{a}}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{3 l}{4 \mathrm{~g}}} \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{T}^{\prime} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\mathrm{~g}}}\right) \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{T}^{\prime} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{~T}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A person measures a time period of a simple pendulum inside a stationary lift and finds it to be $T$. If the lift starts accelerating upwards with an acceleration $\left(\frac{g}{3}\right)$, the time period of the pendulum will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Time period of simple pendulum inside a stationary lift,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where, $I=$ length of string</prep-p>
<prep-p>and $g=$ gravitational acceleration</prep-p>
<prep-p>Acceleration of lift in upward direction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$a=\frac{g}{3}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore$ Time period of pendulum,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { d of pendulum, } \\
\begin{aligned}
T^{\prime} & =2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g+a}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g+\frac{g}{3}}} \\
& =2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{3l}{4 g}}=2 \pi \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} T \text { [from Eq. (i)] }
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A simple pendulum starts oscillating simple harmonically from its mean position ( $\mathrm{x}=0$ ) with amplitude ' $a$ ' and periodic time ' $T$ '. The magnitude of velocity of pendulum at $x=\frac{a}{2}$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Standard expression for velocity in SHM</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For SHM:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x(t) = a \sin(\omega t) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>or equivalently,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v = \frac{dx}{dt} = \omega \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}, $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>where $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Put $x = \tfrac{a}{2}$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ v = \omega \sqrt{a^2 - \left(\frac{a}{2}\right)^2} = \omega \sqrt{a^2 - \frac{a^2}{4}} = \omega \sqrt{\frac{3a^2}{4}}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v = \omega \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} a. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Express $\omega$ in terms of $T$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v = \frac{2\pi}{T} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} a = \frac{\sqrt{3}\pi a}{T}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Compare with options</prep-h3>
<prep-p>This matches <prep-strong>Option D</prep-strong>:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi a}{T}} $</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A particle starts oscillating simple harmonically from its mean position with time period ' $T$ '. At time $\mathrm{t}=\frac{\mathrm{T}}{6}$, the ratio of the potential energy to kinetic energy of the particle is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \left[\sin 30^{\circ}=\cos 60^{\circ}=0 \cdot 5, \cos 30^{\circ}=\sin 60^{\circ}=\sqrt{3} / 2\right] $$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\text { For SHM, }\\ &\begin{aligned} & \text { P.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(i)\\ & \text { and K.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(ii)\\ & \text { Given } t=\frac{T}{6} \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad x & =A \sin \omega t=A \sin \frac{2 \pi}{T} \cdot t \\ \therefore \quad x & =A \sin \frac{2 \pi}{T} \times \frac{T}{6} \\ & =A \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3} A}{2} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(iii)\end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting equation (iii) in equation (i),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \text { P.E. } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~A}^2}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{3 m \omega^2 \mathrm{~A}^2}{8} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting equation (iii) in equation (ii),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \text { K.E. } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-\frac{3 A^2}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(\frac{A^2}{4}\right) \\ \therefore \quad \frac{\text { P.E. }}{\text { K.E. }} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \times \frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \times \frac{1}{4}}=\frac{3}{1} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle starts oscillating simple harmonically from its equilibrium position with time period ' T '. What is the ratio of potential energy to kinetic energy of the particle at time $t=\frac{T}{12}$ ? $$\left(\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\right)$$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For SHM,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { P.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 \quad\text{.... (i)}\\
& \text { and K.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \quad\text{.... (ii)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given $\mathrm{t}=\frac{\mathrm{T}}{12}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad x & =A \sin \omega t=A \sin \frac{2 \pi}{T} \cdot t \\
\therefore \quad x & =A \sin \frac{2 \pi}{T} \times \frac{T}{12} \\
& =A \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \\
& =\frac{A}{2}\quad\text{.... (iii)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting equation (iii) in equation (i),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { P.E. } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(\frac{\mathrm{~A}^2}{4}\right) \\
& =\frac{m \omega^2 A^2}{8}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting equation (iii) in equation (ii),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\text { K.E. } & =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2\left(\mathrm{~A}^2-\frac{\mathrm{A}^2}{4}\right) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~A}^2}{4}\right) \\
\therefore \quad \frac{\text { P.E. }}{\text { K.E. }} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \times \frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \times \frac{3}{4}}=\frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle starts oscillating simple harmonically from its mean position with time period '$$T$$'. At time $$t=\frac{T}{12}$$, the ratio of the potential energy to kinetic energy of the particle is $$\left(\sin 30^{\circ}=\cos 60^{\circ}=0.5, \cos 30^{\circ}=\sin 60^{\circ}=\sqrt{3} / 2\right)$$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-img src="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/fly/@width/image/1lt6157t0/f1ae5c41-88b9-4115-8efc-81d6b740d0d6/120c1840-d659-11ee-a89c-b78526bcb067/file-1lt6157t1.png?format=png" data-orsrc="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/image/1lt6157t0/f1ae5c41-88b9-4115-8efc-81d6b740d0d6/120c1840-d659-11ee-a89c-b78526bcb067/file-1lt6157t1.png" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%;height: auto;display: block;margin: 0 auto;max-height: 40vh;vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2022 11th August Evening Shift Physics - Simple Harmonic Motion Question 110 English Explanation"></prep-p>
<prep-p>The particle starts from the mean position.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{A} \sin \omega \mathrm{t} & =\mathrm{A} \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{\mathrm{T}}\right) \times \mathrm{t} \\
& =A \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{\mathrm{T}} \times \frac{\mathrm{T}}{12}\right) \\
& =A \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{A} \sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2} \quad \therefore \mathrm{x}^2=\frac{\mathrm{A}^2}{4}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore$$ The particle is at a distance $$\mathrm{A} / 2$$ from the mean position.</prep-p>
<prep-p>At this point its P.E. $$=\frac{1}{2} K x^2=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2\quad \text{...... (1)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>and its K.E. $$=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \mathrm{K}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \omega^2\left(\mathrm{~A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right)\quad \text{..... (2)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \frac{\text { P.E. }(\mathrm{U})}{\text { K.E. }(\mathrm{K})}=\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\mathrm{~A}^2-\mathrm{x}^2}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{A}^2}{4}}{\mathrm{~A}^2-\frac{\mathrm{A}^2}{4}}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{A}^2}{4}}{\frac{3 \mathrm{~A}^2}{4}} \\
& \therefore \frac{\mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{K}}=\frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The maximum velocity and maximum acceleration of a particle performing a linear S.H.M. is ' $\alpha$ ' and ' $\beta$ ' respectively. Then the path length of the particle is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For S.H.M.,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Maximum velocity, $\alpha=\mathrm{A} \omega$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\omega=\frac{\alpha}{A}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Maximum acceleration, $\beta=\mathrm{A} \omega^2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \beta=A\left(\frac{\alpha}{A}\right)^2=\frac{\alpha^2}{A} \\
& \Rightarrow A=\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore\quad$ Path length $=2 A=\frac{2 \alpha^2}{\beta}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The displacement of a particle performing S.H.M. is given by $Y=A \cos [\pi(t+\phi)]$. If at $\mathrm{t}=0$, the displacement is $\mathrm{y}=2 \mathrm{~cm}$ and velocity is $2 \pi \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$, the value of amplitude $A$ in cm is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
&\begin{aligned}
& y=A \cos (\pi t+\pi \phi)\\
& v=A \pi \sin (\pi t+\pi \phi) \\
& \text { At } t=0, \frac{y_0}{A}=\cos \pi \phi  \quad\text{.... (i)}\\
& -\frac{v_0}{A}=\sin \pi \phi \quad\text{.... (ii)}
\end{aligned}\\
&\text { Squaring and adding (i) and (ii) }\\
&\mathrm{y}_0^2+\frac{\mathrm{v}_0^2}{\pi^2}=\mathrm{A}^2
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
&\text { Putting } y_0=2 \mathrm{~cm} \text { and } v_0=2 \pi \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}\\
&2^2+\frac{(2 \pi)^2}{\pi^2}=A^2 \quad \Rightarrow A=2 \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The displacement of a particle performing S.H.M. is given by $$x=5 \sin (3 t+3)$$, where $$x$$ is in $$\mathrm{cm}$$ and $$t$$ is in second. The maximum acceleration of the particle will be</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the maximum acceleration of a particle performing Simple Harmonic Motion (S.H.M.), we start with the given displacement function:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$x = 5 \sin (3t + 3)$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Here, $ x $ is in centimeters and $ t $ is in seconds. In S.H.M., the acceleration $ a $ is directly proportional to the displacement $ x $ and is given by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$a = -\omega^2 x$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where $ \omega $ is the angular frequency. From the given displacement equation, we can see that the angular frequency $ \omega $ is 3. Thus, the maximum displacement $ x_{\text{max}} $ is 5 cm because the sine function's amplitude is 5.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The maximum acceleration $ a_{\text{max}} $ occurs when the sine function equals 1 (i.e., at maximum displacement). Hence, we can calculate the maximum acceleration as follows:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$a_{\text{max}} = \omega^2 \cdot x_{\text{max}}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Substituting the values:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$a_{\text{max}} = 3^2 \cdot 5$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$a_{\text{max}} = 9 \cdot 5$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$a_{\text{max}} = 45 \, \mathrm{cm} \, \mathrm{s}^{-2}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus, the maximum acceleration of the particle is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong>: $$45 \, \mathrm{cm} \, \mathrm{s}^{-2}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle performing linear S.H.M. of amplitude $$0.1 \mathrm{~m}$$ has displacement $$0.02 \mathrm{~m}$$ and acceleration $$0.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$$. The maximum velocity of the particle in $$\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$$ is</prep-p>

& \text { Acceleration } \mathrm{a}=\omega^2 \mathrm{x} \\
& \therefore \quad \omega^2=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{x}}=\frac{0.5}{0.02}=25 \\
& \therefore \quad \omega=5 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\
& \quad \mathrm{V}_{\max }=\mathrm{A} \omega^2=0.1 \times 5=0.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Identify the CORRECT decreasing order of basic strength of compounds from following.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Arylamines in general are weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which among the following amines has highest value of $$\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{b}}$$ ?</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which of the following amine is weakest base?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>When comparing the basicity of different amines, it's essential to consider the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom for protonation. This availability is affected by several factors, including inductive effects from alkyl groups and resonance effects.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Let’s analyze each option:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A: Trimethyl amine</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>Trimethyl amine has three methyl groups attached to the nitrogen. Methyl groups are electron-donating through the inductive effect, which increases the electron density on the nitrogen, making it more basic.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: Methyl amine</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>Methyl amine has one methyl group attached to the nitrogen. The electron-donating effect from the single methyl group increases the electron density on nitrogen, but to a lesser extent than trimethyl amine.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: Diethyl amine</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>Diethyl amine has two ethyl groups attached to the nitrogen. Similar to methyl groups, ethyl groups are also electron-donating, which increases the electron density on the nitrogen, making it more basic.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: Aniline</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>Aniline has a phenyl group attached to the nitrogen. The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen in aniline is delocalized over the benzene ring through resonance. This delocalization decreases the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen for protonation, making aniline less basic compared to the aliphatic amines mentioned above.</prep-p>

<prep-p>In summary, the basicity order based on the availability of the lone pair on nitrogen is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Diethyl amine > Trimethyl amine > Methyl amine > Aniline</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the weakest base among the given options is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: Aniline</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which of the following amines acts as strongest base?</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:

<prep-p>$$\therefore \mathrm{(CH_3)_2 NH}$$ acts as strong base.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The value of $\int_0^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x$ is (where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer function not greater than $x$ )</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content: <prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \int_0^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x \\ & =\int_0^1\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x+\int_1^{\sqrt{2}}\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}}\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x+\int_{\sqrt{3}}^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x \\ & =\int_0^1 0 \mathrm{~d} x+\int_1^{\sqrt{2}} 1 \mathrm{~d} x+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}} 2 \mathrm{~d} x+\int_{\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{2}} 3 \mathrm{~d} x \\ & =0+1(\sqrt{2}-1)+2(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})+3(2-\sqrt{3}) \\ & =\sqrt{2}-1+2 \sqrt{3}-2 \sqrt{2}+6-3 \sqrt{3} \\ & =5-\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>$$\int_\limits{0.2}^{3.5}[x] \mathrm{d} x=$$

(where $[x]=$ greatest integer not greater than $x$ )</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\int_\limits0^2[x] \mathrm{d} x+\int_\limits0^2|x-1| \mathrm{d} x=$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>(where $$[x]$$ denotes the greatest integer function.)</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To evaluate the given integrals, let's tackle them one by one.</prep-p>

<prep-p>First, let's evaluate the integral with the greatest integer function (also known as the floor function), $$\int_\limits0^2[x] \mathrm{d} x$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The greatest integer function $$[x]$$ returns the greatest integer less than or equal to $$x$$. On the interval from 0 to 2, $$[x]$$ takes on the values 0 and 1. Specifically:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>For $$0 \le x < 1, [x] = 0$$</prep-li>
<prep-li>For $$1 \le x < 2, [x] = 1$$</prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p>Hence, the integral of the greatest integer function can be separated into two integrals:</prep-p>

$$\int_\limits0^2[x] \mathrm{d} x = \int_\limits0^1 0\,\mathrm{d} x + \int_\limits1^2 1\,\mathrm{d} x$$

<prep-p>Evaluating these integrals, we get:</prep-p>

$$= \big(0 \cdot x\big) \Big|_0^1 + \big(x\big) \Big|_1^2$$

$$= (0 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0) + (2 - 1)$$

$$= 0 + 1$$

$$= 1$$

<prep-p>Next, let's evaluate the integral of the absolute value function, $$\int_\limits0^2|x-1| \mathrm{d} x$$.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The absolute function $$|x - 1|$$ equals $$x - 1$$ when $$x \ge 1$$ and equals $$-x + 1$$ when $$x < 1$$. Consequently, the integral can be separated at the point where $$x = 1$$:</prep-p>

$$\int_\limits0^2|x-1| \mathrm{d} x = \int_\limits0^1(-x+1) \mathrm{d} x + \int_\limits1^2(x-1) \mathrm{d} x$$

<prep-p>Evaluating the first part of the integral:</prep-p>

$$\int_\limits0^1(-x+1) \mathrm{d} x = \left(-\frac{x^2}{2} + x\right) \Big|_0^1$$

$$= \left(-\frac{1^2}{2} + 1\right) - \left(-\frac{0^2}{2} + 0\right)$$

$$= (-\frac{1}{2} + 1) - 0$$

$$= \frac{1}{2}$$

<prep-p>Now, evaluating the second part:</prep-p>

$$\int_\limits1^2(x-1) \mathrm{d} x = \left(\frac{x^2}{2} - x\right) \Big|_1^2$$

$$= \left(\frac{2^2}{2} - 2\right) - \left(\frac{1^2}{2} - 1\right)$$

$$= (2 - 2) - (\frac{1}{2} - 1)$$

$$= 0 - (-\frac{1}{2})$$

$$= \frac{1}{2}$$

<prep-p>Adding the results of both parts of the absolute value integral:</prep-p>

$$\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1$$

<prep-p>Finally, combining the results from both original integrals:</prep-p>

$$\int_\limits0^2[x] \mathrm{d} x+\int_\limits0^2|x-1| \mathrm{d} x = 1 + 1 = 2$$

<prep-p>Therefore, the correct answer is Option D, which is 2.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Identify the defect developed when an ion of an ionic compound is missing from its regular site and occupies interstitial position between lattice points.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The defect described is when an <prep-strong>ion is missing from its regular lattice site and instead occupies an interstitial position</prep-strong>.  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Schottky defect</prep-strong> → Involves missing cations and anions, creating vacancies, but no interstitial occupation.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Frenkel defect</prep-strong> → In this defect, an ion (usually a smaller cation) leaves its normal lattice site and occupies an interstitial position.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Substitutional impurity defect</prep-strong> → Involves replacement of some ions by different ions of similar size.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Interstitial impurity defect</prep-strong> → Involves the introduction of foreign atoms/ions in interstitial sites.  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>✅ Correct Answer: <prep-strong>Option B: Frenkel defect</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Identify the type of defect from following in stainless steel.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Stainless steel is an alloy in which smaller atoms like carbon or nitrogen occupy the interstitial sites of the iron lattice.</prep-p>
<prep-p>This is called an <prep-strong>interstitial impurity defect</prep-strong>, where foreign atoms occupy the voids (interstitial sites) between the host metal atoms.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Option B  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Interstitial impurity defect</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an ionic solid equal number of cations and anions are missing from their regular positions in the crystal lattice creating vacancies is called-</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content: <prep-p><prep-strong>Schottky defect</prep-strong> is the term used when equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their regular positions in the crystal lattice of an ionic solid, thereby creating vacancies. This type of defect is common in ionic compounds with high coordination numbers and similar-sized cations and anions. The loss or absence of these ion pairs maintains the electrical neutrality and decreases the density of the crystal.</prep-p>

</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate van't Hoff factor (i) of 0.2 m aqueous solution of an electrolyte if it freezes at $-0.660 \mathrm{~K} .\left(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=1.84 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To calculate the van't Hoff factor ($i$), we can use the formula for freezing point depression:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta T_f = i \cdot K_f \cdot m $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$\Delta T_f$ is the depression in the freezing point,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$i$ is the van't Hoff factor,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$K_f$ is the freezing point depression constant,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$m$ is the molality of the solution.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>From the problem, we know:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$\Delta T_f = 0.660 \, \mathrm{K}$,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$K_f = 1.84 \, \mathrm{K \, kg \, mol^{-1}}$,</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$m = 0.2 \, \mathrm{mol \, kg^{-1}}$.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>We can rearrange the formula to solve for $i$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ i = \frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f \cdot m} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the given values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ i = \frac{0.660}{1.84 \times 0.2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ i = \frac{0.660}{0.368} \approx 1.79 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The van't Hoff factor for this solution is approximately 1.79. Therefore, the correct option is <prep-strong>Option B: 1.79</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: The average force applied on the walls of a closed container depends as $\mathrm{T}^{\mathrm{x}}$ where T is the temperature of an ideal gas. The value of $x$ is
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let us solve the problem step by step.</prep-p>
<prep-ol>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Pressure of an Ideal Gas:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>According to the kinetic theory of gases, the pressure ($P$) exerted by an ideal gas is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    P = \frac{1}{3} \frac{N m \langle v^2 \rangle}{V}    $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$N$ = number of molecules,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$m$ = mass of one molecule,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\langle v^2 \rangle$ = mean square speed,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$V$ = volume.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Kinetic Energy and Temperature:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The average kinetic energy of one molecule is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    \frac{1}{2} m \langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2} k_B T    $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    m \langle v^2 \rangle = 3 k_B T    $$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Expressing Pressure in Terms of Temperature:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the value from step 2 into the pressure equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    P = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{N}{V} \cdot (3 k_B T)    $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    P = \frac{N}{V} k_B T    $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a fixed number of molecules and volume, $N$ and $V$ are constant.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Force on the Walls:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Pressure ($P$) is force ($F$) per unit area ($A$). So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$    P = \frac{F}{A} \implies F = P \cdot A    $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a given container (fixed area), $F \propto P$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Dependence on Temperature:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>From above, $P \propto T$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $F \propto T$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Value of $x$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Force on walls $\propto T^x$,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $x = 1$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ol>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Option A  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\boxed{1}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The average force applied on the wall of a closed container depends as $\mathrm{T}^{\mathrm{x}}$ where T is the temperature of an ideal gas. The value of $x$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The average force applied on the wall of a closed container can be related to the temperature of an ideal gas using its dependency on temperature $ \mathrm{T}^{\mathrm{x}} $. To find the value of $ x $, we can derive it step by step:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>The pressure $ P $ is defined as force $ F $ per unit area $ A $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    P = \frac{F}{A}    $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, pressure is proportional to force:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    P \propto F \quad \text{.... (i)}    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>According to the ideal gas law, the pressure $ P $ is also given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    P = \frac{nRT}{V}    $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $ n $ is the number of moles, $ R $ is the ideal gas constant, $ T $ is the temperature, and $ V $ is the volume. If the volume $ V $ is constant:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    P \propto T \quad \text{.... (ii)}    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Combining equations (i) and (ii), we find the relationship between force and temperature:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    F \propto T^x    $</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>From the proportionality derived:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$  x = 1  $</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The average force applied on the walls of a closed container depends on $$T^x$$ where $$T$$ is the temperature of an ideal gas. The value of '$$x$$' is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& P=\frac{F}{A} \\
\therefore \quad P & \propto F \quad \text{..... (i)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>From Ideal Gas Equation,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{P}=\frac{\mathrm{nRT}}{\mathrm{V}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>When V remains constant,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{P} \propto \mathrm{T}$$ ..... (ii)</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$\mathrm{F} \propto \mathrm{T}^{\mathrm{x}}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In Paschen series, wavelength of first line is ' $\lambda_1$ ' and for Brackett series, wavelength of first line is ' $\lambda_2$ ' then ratio $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Using Rydberg's formula,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_1^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_2^2}\right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For Paschen series, $\mathrm{n}_1=3$ and $\mathrm{n}_2=4$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=R\left(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{7 R}{16 \times 9} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For Brackett series,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{n}_1=4 \text { and } \mathrm{n}_2=5 \\ & \frac{1}{\lambda_2}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{25}\right)=\frac{9 \mathrm{R}}{16 \times 25} \\ & \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{9 \mathrm{R}}{16 \times 25} \times \frac{16 \times 9}{7 \mathrm{R}}=\frac{81}{175} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In Balmer series, wavelength of the $$2^{\text {nd }}$$ line is '$$\lambda_1$$' and for Paschen series, wavelength of the $$1^{\text {st }}$$ line is '$$\lambda_2$$', then the ratio '$$\lambda_1$$' to '$$\lambda_2$$' is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For spectral series, $$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R Z^2\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_1^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_2^2}\right)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For the Balmer series, $$\mathrm{n}_1=2$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The wavelength for $$2^{\text {nd }}$$ line of the Balmer series is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=\mathrm{RZ}^2\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right) \\
& \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=\mathrm{RZ}^2\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right) \\
& \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=\mathrm{RZ}^2\left(\frac{3}{16}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda_1=\left[\frac{16}{3}\right]
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For the Paschen series, $$\mathrm{n}_1=3$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The wavelength for $$1^{\text {st }}$$ line of the Paschen series is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{\lambda_2} & =R Z^2\left(\frac{1}{3^2}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right) \\
\frac{1}{\lambda_2} & =R Z^2\left(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16}\right) \\
\lambda_2 & =\frac{144}{7} \\
\frac{1}{\lambda_2} & =R Z^2\left(\frac{7}{144}\right) \\
\therefore \quad \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} & =\frac{16}{3} \times \frac{7}{144}=\frac{7}{27}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>In Balmer series, wavelength of first line is ' $\lambda_1$ ' and in Brackett series wavelength of first line is ' $\lambda_2$ ' then $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The wavelength of a line in Balmer series is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\quad [\text{for } n=3,4,5, \ldots]$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where, $R=$ Rydberg constant.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first line, $n=3$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda_1=\frac{36}{5 R}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The wavelength of a line in Brackett series is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{4^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\quad \text{for } n=5,6,7 \ldots$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first line, $n=5$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{\lambda_2}=R\left(\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{25}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda_2=\frac{400}{9 R}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{36}{5 R} \times \frac{9 R}{400}=\frac{81}{500}=0.162$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The solubility product of AgBr is $4.9 \times 10^{-13}$ at a certain temperature. Calculate the solubility.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We are given:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_{sp}(\text{AgBr}) = 4.9 \times 10^{-13} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Dissociation Equation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{AgBr (s)} \; \rightleftharpoons \; \text{Ag}^+ (aq) + \text{Br}^- (aq) $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Expression for $K_{sp}$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>If solubility = $s$ mol dm$^{-3}$, then:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ [\text{Ag}^+] = s, \quad [\text{Br}^-] = s $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_{sp} = s \times s = s^2 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Solve for $s$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ s = \sqrt{K_{sp}} = \sqrt{4.9 \times 10^{-13}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ s = \sqrt{4.9} \times 10^{-6.5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, $\sqrt{4.9} \approx 2.21$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Also, $10^{-6.5} = 10^{-7} \cdot \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16 \times 10^{-7}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ s \approx 2.21 \times 3.16 \times 10^{-7} \approx 6.98 \times 10^{-7} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{Solubility} \approx 7 \times 10^{-7} \, \text{mol dm}^{-3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: C</prep-strong> ✅</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The solubility of AgBr is $7.1 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{dm}^{-3}$. Calculate its solubility product at the same temperature.</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content: <prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{ll}  & \mathrm{AgBr}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+}+\mathrm{Br}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{-} \\ \therefore \quad & x=1, y=1 \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=x^x y^y \mathrm{~S}^{x+y}=(1)^1(1)^1 \mathrm{~S}^{1+1}=\mathrm{S}^2 \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=\left(7.1 \times 10^{-7}\right)^2=5.04 \times 10^{-13} \end{array} $$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: The solubility product of a sparingly soluble salt AX is $4.9 \times 10^{-13}$. What is its solubility in $\mathrm{mol} \mathrm{dm}^{-3}$ ?
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let the sparingly soluble salt be $ AX $.</prep-p>
<prep-p>When $ AX $ dissolves in water, it dissociates as:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ AX (s) \rightleftharpoons A^+ (aq) + X^- (aq) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let the solubility of $ AX $ be $ S $ mol.dm$^{-3}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>At equilibrium:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$[A^+] = S$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$[X^-] = S$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>The solubility product expression is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_{sp} = [A^+][X^-] $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_{sp} = S \times S = S^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_{sp} = 4.9 \times 10^{-13} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S^2 = 4.9 \times 10^{-13} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Taking square root on both sides:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S = \sqrt{4.9 \times 10^{-13}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S = \sqrt{4.9} \times \sqrt{10^{-13}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S = 2.2136 \times 10^{-6.5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 10^{-6.5} = 10^{-6} \times 10^{-0.5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>And,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 10^{-0.5} \approx 0.316 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S = 2.2136 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.316 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S = 0.7 \times 10^{-6} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ S = 7.0 \times 10^{-7} \ \text{mol dm}^{-3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: $ 7.0 \times 10^{-7} $ mol dm$^{-3}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>When a metallic surface is illuminated with a radiation of wavelength ' $\lambda$ ', the stopping potential is ' $V$ '. If the same surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength ' $3 \lambda$ ', the stopping potential is ' $\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}}{6}\right)$ '. The threshold wavelength for the surface is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { From Einstein's equation, } \\
& \mathrm{hv}=\mathrm{e} \mathrm{V}_0+\mathrm{h} v_0 \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}=e \mathrm{~V}_0 \\
& \text { case (i) } \lambda=\lambda ; \mathrm{V}_0=\mathrm{V} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}=\mathrm{eV}\quad\text{... (i)} \\
& \text { case (ii) } \lambda=3 \lambda ; \mathrm{V}_0=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{6} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{hc}}{3 \lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}=\frac{\mathrm{eV}}{6} \quad\text{... (ii)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore\quad & \frac{\left(\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{3 \lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}\right)}=6 \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}=6\left(\frac{1}{3 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}=\frac{2}{\lambda}-\frac{6}{\lambda_0} \\
\therefore & \frac{-1}{\lambda_0}+\frac{6}{\lambda_0}=\frac{2}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda} \\
\therefore & \frac{5}{\lambda_0}=\frac{1}{\lambda} \Rightarrow \lambda_0=5 \lambda
\end{array}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>When radiation of wavelength '$$\lambda$$' is incident on a metallic surface, the stopping potential is 4.8 V. If the surface is illuminated with radiation of double the wavelength then the stopping potential becomes $$1.6 \mathrm{~V}$$. The threshold wavelength for the surface is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Stopping potential:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{eV}_0=\mathrm{h} \nu-\phi_0 \\
& \mathrm{eV}_0=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\phi_0
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For first case: $$e(4.8)=\frac{h c}{\lambda}-\phi_0$$ ..... (i)</prep-p>
<prep-p>For Second case: $$e(1.6)=\frac{h c}{2 \lambda}-\phi_0$$ ..... (ii)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Dividing equation (i) by equation (ii),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$3\left(\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{2 \lambda}-\phi_0\right)=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\phi_0$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & \frac{3 \mathrm{hc}}{2 \lambda}-3 \phi_0=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\phi_0 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{hc}}{2 \lambda}=2 \phi_0 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{hc}}{4 \lambda}=\phi_0
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad$$ Threshold wavelength is $$4 \lambda$$.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>When a metallic surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength '$$\lambda$$', the stopping potential is '$$\mathrm{V}$$'. If the same surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength '$$2 \lambda$$', the stopping potential is '$$\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{4}\right)$$'. The threshold wavelength for the metallic surface is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For stopping potential $$\mathrm{V}, \mathrm{eV}=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For stopping potential $$\frac{\mathrm{V}}{4}, \frac{\mathrm{eV}}{4}=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{2 \lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda_0}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Taking the ratio, we get</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& 4=\frac{\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)}{\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}} \\
& 4\left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)=\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0} \\
& \left(\frac{2}{\lambda}-\frac{4}{\lambda_0}\right)=\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0} \\
& \left(\frac{2}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)=-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}+\frac{4}{\lambda_0} \\
& \quad\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)=\frac{3}{\lambda_0} \\
& \therefore \quad \lambda_0=3 \lambda
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>When a capacitor is connected in series LR circuit, the alternating current flowing in the circuit</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We are given an LR circuit (an <prep-strong>inductor & resistor in series</prep-strong>).  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, a capacitor is connected in series with it, making it an <prep-strong>LCR series circuit</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Analysis:</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>In an <prep-strong>LR circuit</prep-strong>, the impedance is  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   Z_{LR} = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}   $</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>If a capacitor is added in series, the impedance becomes:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   Z_{LCR} = \sqrt{R^2 + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2}   $</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Clearly, the impedance <prep-strong>does not remain constant</prep-strong>; it depends on frequency and C.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>If $\omega L = \tfrac{1}{\omega C}$, i.e. the circuit is in resonance, the reactances cancel each other, so:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   Z = R   $  </prep-p>
<prep-p>This is <prep-strong>smaller</prep-strong> than the LR impedance $Z_{LR}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the current in the circuit <prep-strong>increases</prep-strong>.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>So in general, adding the capacitor provides a possibility of cancelling out some inductive reactance, thereby reducing impedance and <prep-strong>increasing the current</prep-strong>.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>✅ Correct Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B — increases</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>When a capacitor is connected in series LR circuit, the alternating current flowing in the circuit</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Impedance in LR circuit,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{Z}=\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}{ }^2}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Impedance in LCR circuit,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{Z}=\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^2+\left(\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}-\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}\right)^2}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ When capacitor is connected in series, Z decreases.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$I=\frac{V}{Z} \Rightarrow I \propto \frac{1}{Z}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ When $Z$ decreases, $I$ increases.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Which graph shows the correct variation of r.m.s. current 'I' with frequency 'f' of a.c. in case of (LCR) parallel resonance circuit?</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-img src="https://mkvdpokqofzstcoifhzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/pyq-images/Physics/4362.jpg" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%;height: auto;display: block;margin: 0 auto;max-height: 40vh;vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2021 24th September Morning Shift Physics - Alternating Current Question 111 English"></prep-p>
The instantaneous value of current in an a.c. circuit is $I=3 \sin \left(50 \pi t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \mathrm{A}$. The current will be maximum for the first time at
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given equation of instantaneous current:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ I = 3 \sin \left(50\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \text{ A} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The current will be <prep-strong>maximum</prep-strong> when the value of $\sin$ is $1$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 50\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, solve for $t$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 50\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Subtract $\frac{\pi}{4}$ from both sides:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 50\pi t = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 50\pi t = \frac{2\pi - \pi}{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 50\pi t = \frac{\pi}{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide both sides by $50\pi$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t = \frac{\pi}{4} \div 50\pi $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{50} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t = \frac{1}{200} \text{ s} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option is:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong> $\boxed{\frac{1}{200}~\mathrm{s}}$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A wire has three different sections as shown in figure. The magnitude of the magnetic field produced at the centre ' $O$ ' of the semicircle by three sections together is ( $\mu_0=$ permiability of free space)</prep-p><prep-img src="https://mkvdpokqofzstcoifhzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/pyq-images/Physics/3905.jpg" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 20th April Morning Shift Physics - Moving Charges and Magnetism Question 30 English">
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let's analyse each wire section's contribution to magnetic field at centre $O$:</prep-p>
<prep-h3>1. <prep-strong>Straight Segment AB</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a straight wire passing through the centre, and with infinite length, field at the centre is <prep-strong>zero</prep-strong> by symmetry because the contributions from both sides cancel. The segment AB is straight and passes directly through $O$, so:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ B_{AB} = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>2. <prep-strong>Semicircular Section BC</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>Magnetic field at centre, due to a current $I$ in a <prep-strong>semicircular arc of radius $R$</prep-strong> is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ B_{BC} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Direction: Using <prep-strong>right hand rule</prep-strong>, direction is <prep-strong>into the page</prep-strong> (or use NCERT convention, if you imagine current flowing from B to C).</prep-p>

<prep-h3>3. <prep-strong>Straight Segment CD</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>Again, this is a straight segment passing through $O$, so its field at $O$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ B_{CD} = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>4. <prep-strong>Total Magnetic Field at $O$</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>Adding all three contributions:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ B_{\text{total}} = B_{AB} + B_{BC} + B_{CD} = 0 + \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R} + 0 = \boxed{\frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\text{Option A: } \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}} $</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content:
Two long parallel wires carrying currents 4 A and 3 A in opposite directions are placed at a distance of 5 cm from each other. A point P is at equidistance from both the wires such that the line joining the point P to the wires are perpendicular to each other. The magnitude of magnetic field at point $P$ is
( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space $=4 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-img src="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/fly/@width/image/jaoe38c1meqoieq4/67e6c1ad-49ca-4fb4-a88f-d7881ff2ebb8/aad3c4c0-8174-11f0-981d-5fb8ef89fe94/file-jaoe38c1meqoieq5.png?format=png" data-orsrc="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/image/jaoe38c1meqoieq4/67e6c1ad-49ca-4fb4-a88f-d7881ff2ebb8/aad3c4c0-8174-11f0-981d-5fb8ef89fe94/file-jaoe38c1meqoieq5.png" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 19th April Morning Shift Physics - Moving Charges and Magnetism Question 33 English Explanation"></prep-p>
<prep-p>Magnetic field produced by two wires</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{B}_1=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}_1}{2 \pi \mathrm{X}} \text { and } \mathrm{B}_2=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}_2}{2 \pi \mathrm{X}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>From Figure,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{net}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{B}_1^2+\mathrm{B}_2^2}=\frac{\mu_0}{2 \pi \mathrm{X}} \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1^2+\mathrm{I}_2^2}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Also, using Pythagoras theorem, $2 \mathrm{X}^2=5 \times 5$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore & X=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~cm} \\
& B_{\text {net }}=\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7}}{2 \pi \times \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}} \sqrt{4^2+3^2}=2 \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two circular coils made from same wire but radius of $$1^{\text {st }}$$ coil is twice that of $$2^{\text {nd }}$$ coil. & \therefore \quad \frac{I_1}{I_2}=2 \quad \text{.... (i)}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The resistance through the coil,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\mathrm{R} \propto l$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, $$l=2 \pi \mathrm{r}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{r}_1}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}_2}=2 \quad \text{.... (ii)}\\
& \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_1 \mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{I}_2 \mathrm{R}_2}=2 \times 2=4 \quad \text{...[From (i) and (ii)]}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A bar magnet has length 4 cm , cross-sectional area $2 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ and magnetic moment $6 \mathrm{Am}^2$. The intensity of magnetisation of bar magnet is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
&\text { Intensity of magnetization }\\
&\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{M_{\text {nat }}}{\text { Volume }} \\
& =\frac{M_{\text {net }}}{\text { length } \times \text { area of cross-section }} \\
& =\frac{6}{\left(4 \times 10^{-2}\right) \times\left(2 \times 10^{-1}\right)}=7.5 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{m}

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A bar magnet has length $$3 \mathrm{~cm}$$, cross-sectional area $$2 \mathrm{~cm}^2$$ and magnetic moment $$3 \mathrm{~Am}^2$$. The intensity of magnetisation of bar magnet is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the intensity of magnetization (I) of the bar magnet, we can use the formula:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$I = \frac{M}{V}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where $M$ is the magnetic moment and $V$ is the volume of the bar magnet. The volume can be obtained using the length ($l$) and the cross-sectional area ($A$) of the bar magnet:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$V = A \cdot l$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Given that the length of the bar magnet $l$ is $3 \, \mathrm{cm} = 3 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{m}$ and the cross-sectional area $A$ is $2 \, \mathrm{cm}^2 = 2 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{m}^2$, we can calculate the volume as:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$V = 2 \times 10^{-4} \, \mathrm{m}^2 \times 3 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{m} = 6 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{m}^3$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now, substituting the given magnetic moment $M = 3 \, \mathrm{Am}^2$ and the calculated volume into the intensity of magnetization formula, we get:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$I = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{3 \, \mathrm{Am}^2}{6 \times 10^{-6} \, \mathrm{m}^3} = \frac{3}{6 \times 10^{-6}} \, \mathrm{A/m} = \frac{1}{2 \times 10^{-6}} \, \mathrm{A/m} = 0.5 \times 10^6 \, \mathrm{A/m} = 5 \times 10^5 \, \mathrm{A/m}$$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the correct answer is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option D</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$5 \times 10^5 \, \mathrm{A/m}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>The magnetization of bar magnet of length 5 cm , cross sectional area $2 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ and net magnetic moment $1 \mathrm{Am}^2$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
l & =5 \mathrm{~cm}=5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m} \\
a & =2 \mathrm{~cm}^2=2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2 \\
\text{and}\quad M & =1 \mathrm{Am}^{-2}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The magnetisation of the bar magnet is given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$I=\frac{M}{V}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where, $\quad V=$ volume of bar magnet $=a \times l$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Rightarrow \quad I=\frac{M}{a \times l}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting given values, we get</prep-p>

& =1 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{m}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>When a diatomic gas (rigid) undergoes adiabatic change, its pressure $(\mathrm{P})$ and temperature $(\mathrm{T})$ are related as $P \propto T^c$. The value of $c$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a <prep-strong>rigid diatomic gas</prep-strong> (meaning rotation is allowed but vibration is ignored), we proceed as per the NCERT method.</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Step 1: Adiabatic Equation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For any adiabatic process:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ PV^\gamma = \text{constant} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $\gamma$ is the adiabatic index.</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Step 2: Ideal Gas Law</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Also,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ PV = nRT $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V = \frac{nRT}{P} $$</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Step 3: Substitute $V$ in adiabatic equation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Substitute $V$ in the adiabatic equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P\left( \frac{nRT}{P} \right)^\gamma = \text{constant} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P \cdot (nRT)^\gamma \cdot P^{-\gamma} = \text{constant} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (nR)^\gamma \cdot P^{1-\gamma} \cdot T^\gamma = \text{constant} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $n$ and $R$ are constants, we can absorb them into the overall constant:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P^{1-\gamma} \cdot T^\gamma = \text{constant} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P^{1-\gamma} \propto T^{-\gamma} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P \propto T^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}} $</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Step 4: Value of $\gamma$ for Diatomic Gas</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas (rotational but <prep-strong>not vibrational</prep-strong>):</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Degrees of freedom $= 5$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$C_v = \frac{5}{2} R$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$C_p = C_v + R = \frac{7}{2}R$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \frac{7/2}{5/2} = \frac{7}{5} = 1.4$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-h3>Step 5: Value of $c$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$\displaystyle P \propto T^c\ \qquad\text{where}\ c = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\gamma = \frac{7}{5}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ c = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{7}{5} - 1} = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{2}{5}} = \frac{7}{2} = 3.5 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct answer: Option B (3.5)</prep-strong></prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A diatomic gas undergoes adiabatic change. Its pressure P and temperature T are related as $\mathrm{P} \propto \mathrm{T}^{\mathrm{x}}$ where the value of x is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas undergoing an adiabatic process, the relationship between pressure ($P$) and temperature ($T$) can be derived using the adiabatic condition and the gas law.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The adiabatic condition for an ideal gas is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $P$ is pressure, $V$ is volume, and $\gamma$ (gamma) is the adiabatic index or heat capacity ratio given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas, the degrees of freedom $ f $ are 5, so:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ C_v = \frac{f}{2}R = \frac{5}{2}R $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ C_p = C_v + R = \frac{7}{2}R $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \frac{\frac{7}{2}R}{\frac{5}{2}R} = \frac{7}{5} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The ideal gas law is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ PV = nRT $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>During an adiabatic process, we also have:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P \propto V^{-\gamma} $$ </prep-p>
<prep-p>and </prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T \propto V^{\gamma-1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the relationship for temperature:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>From the ideal gas law $PV = nRT$, we have $P = \frac{nRT}{V}$.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>We can substitute $T \propto V^{\gamma-1}$ into the ideal gas law:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P \propto \left(V^{\gamma-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{V}} \Rightarrow P \propto \left(V^{1-\gamma}\right) $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Hence, $P \propto T^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}$.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Plugging in the value of γ for a diatomic gas:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \gamma = \frac{7}{5} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1} = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{7}{5}-1} = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{2}{5}} = \frac{7}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, for a diatomic gas, the relationship is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P \propto T^{\frac{7}{2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the value of $ x $ is $ 3.5 $. </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Answer:</prep-strong> Option A, $ x = 3.5 $.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>A diatomic gas undergoes adiabatic change. Its pressure $$p$$ and temperature $$T$$ are related as $$p \propto T^x$$, where $$x$$ is</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas undergoing an adiabatic change, the relationship between pressure ($p$) and temperature ($T$) is defined by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{T^\gamma}{p^{\gamma-1}} = \text{constant}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This equation can be rearranged to:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$T^\gamma = \text{constant} \times p^{\gamma - 1}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>By simplifying further, we find:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$p \propto T^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given that $p \propto T^x$, we equate the exponents:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$x = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas, the adiabatic index $\gamma$ is $\frac{7}{5}$. Substituting this value, we calculate:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$x = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{7}{5} - 1}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This simplifies to:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$x = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{2}{5}} = \frac{7}{2} = 3.5$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, for a diatomic gas undergoing an adiabatic process, the value of $x$ is 3.5.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>An insulated container contains a diatomic gas of molar mass ' m '. The container is moving with velocity ' $V$ ', if it is stopped suddenly, the change in temperature is ( $R=$ gas constant)</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>In an insulated container containing a diatomic gas with molar mass 'm', moving at velocity 'V', if the container is stopped suddenly, the change in temperature can be calculated as follows:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Kinetic Energy (K.E.) of the Gas:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The kinetic energy of the gas is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \text{K.E.} = n \left( \frac{1}{2} m V^2 \right)    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Internal Energy Change (ΔU):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>When the container is stopped, the change in internal energy is expressed as:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta U = n C_v \Delta T    $</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas, the specific heat capacity at constant volume is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    C_v = \frac{5}{2} R    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Energy Conservation:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Since energy is conserved when the container is stopped, the change in internal energy equals the initial kinetic energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta U = \text{K.E.}    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Solving for Change in Temperature (ΔT):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the expressions from above, we have:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    n \frac{5}{2} R \Delta T = n \left( \frac{1}{2} m V^2 \right)    $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cancelling 'n' from both sides and solving for ΔT:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta T = \frac{m V^2}{5 R}    $</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>This expression gives the change in temperature of the gas when the container is abruptly stopped.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>An insulated container contains a monoatomic gas of molar mass ' $m$ '. The container is moving with velocity ' $V$ '. If it is stopped suddenly, the change in temperature is ( $R=$ gas constant)</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>When the insulated container, which contains a monoatomic gas with molar mass ' $ m $ ', is suddenly stopped from moving at velocity ' $ V $ ', there is a change in temperature due to the conversion of kinetic energy into internal energy.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>The loss in kinetic energy of the gas is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \frac{1}{2}(\text{mn}) V^2    $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $ n $ is the number of moles of the gas.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>For a monoatomic gas, the change in internal energy is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta \mathrm{U} = \frac{3}{2} \mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>The change in kinetic energy is entirely converted into internal energy, leading to:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \frac{3}{2} n R \Delta T = \frac{1}{2} m n V^2    $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Solving for the change in temperature, $ \Delta T $, we have:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta T = \frac{m V^2}{3 R}    $</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>This equation shows the direct relationship between the change in temperature and the initial velocity of the container, illustrating how kinetic energy influences the internal energy and hence the temperature change in an ideal gaseous system.</prep-p>

questions.pyq_content: <prep-p>An insulated container contains a monoatomic gas of molar mass '$$\mathrm{m}$$'. The container is moving with velocity '$$\mathrm{V}$$'. If it is stopped suddenly, the change in temperature of a gas is [R is gas constant]</prep-p>
questions.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Kinetic energy loss of the gas is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Delta \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} M V^2 \cdot \mathrm{n}$$ ..... (i) ....(where $$\mathrm{n}$$ is the no. of moles of the gas)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Heat  gained by the gas due to temperature change $$\Delta \mathrm{T}$$ is $$\Delta Q={ }_n C_V \Delta T
$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>But, $$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{V}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{R}$$ ....(gas is monoatomic)</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{R} \cdot \mathrm{n} \Delta \mathrm{T}$$ ..... (ii)</prep-p>
<prep-p>Equating (i) and (ii),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \mathrm{E}=\Delta \mathrm{Q} \\
& \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MV}^2 \cdot \mathrm{n}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{R} \cdot \mathrm{n} \Delta \mathrm{T} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{T}=\frac{\mathrm{MV}}{3 \mathrm{R}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
